As a next step in the validation process, input-output checks of the HelicityAmplitude module are performed. For this an amplitude model is constructed that is used for both the data generation and fitting with ComPWA. In this section a simple amplitude was created, using only the f 0 ( 2020 ) and the f 2 ( 1270 ) resonance. The choice of these specific f resonances is based on their strong presence in the BESIII data [ 120 ]. All possible helicities for the occuring states are used, except for the spin projection component of the J/ψ equal to zero, as noted above. In addition a coherently added background term, distributed uniformly in phase space, is introduced.
7 . 3 first validation with a simple model
101
The parameters of the helicity intensity chosen for the data generation are displayed in table 7 . Here the values for the masses and widths of the resonances are taken from the Particle Data Group (PDG) [ 9 ]. In total 600 independent data samples, each with 20000 events, were generated with the the hit-or-miss MC method. For the normalization of the amplitudes in the log-likelihood of the fit, independent phase-space MC data samples with ten times more events are used.
Table 7 : Parameters of the simple model for the reaction J/ψ → γπ 0 π 0 including f 0 , f 2 as intermediate resonances. For the masses and widths of the intermediate resonances the PDG values are used [ 9 ].
Each sample is fitted 7 times with random start values for the fit parameters listed above. The masses and widths are chosen at random from a [-20 , 20 ] % interval around their PDG values. Similarly the start parameters for the magnitudes and phases are random variables of the uniform distributions ranging from [ 0 , 5 ] and [-π , π ] respectively. The coherent phase space magnitude was limited to [ 0 , 0 . 1 ] . As denoted in table 7 the λ = 0 component of the f 2 wave was chosen to be fixed in the fits. This is allowed and needed to stabilize the fitting procedure as explained in the previous chapter. For each data sample only the best fit, based on the likelihood value, was selected and used further. This procedure increases the probability of having found the global minimum.
At first the kinematic distributions of the generated datasets and their fit results can be compared. For this, one of the 600 samples with its best fit result was chosen at random. To visualize the helicity intensity of this fit result another data sample was produced using the weighted MC method. A good overview of the goodness-of-fit is given by the Dalitz plot comparison, which is shown in figure 66 2 .
From the Dalitz plot of the input data (hit-or-miss MC), the two resonances in the π 0 π 0 subsystem can be seen nicely. This is indicated by the two bands at around 1 . 7 GeV 2 /c 4 and 4 GeV 2 /c 4 . Also their spin properties can be identified when comparing the distri- bution along the bands with figures 62 and 64 . While the f 0 state at a higher mass shows no modulation, which is compatible with a spin 0 particle, the f 2 state at the lower mass resembles the angular distribution for a spin 2 particle with λ = 0 . This can be seen from the peaking at the phase space boundaries. However in this case a more distinct bump in the center of the f 2 band should be present. This in turn is explained by the destructive interference of the λ = 0 and λ = 2 waves of the f 2 , which is supported nicely by the parameter values given in table 7 .

As a next step in the validation process, input-output checks of the HelicityAmplitude module are performed. For this an amplitude model is constructed that is used for both the data generation and fitting with ComPWA. In this section a simple amplitude was created, using only the f 0 ( 2020 ) and the f 2 ( 1270 ) resonance. The choice of these specific f resonances is based on their strong presence in the BESIII data [ 120 ]. All possible helicities for the occuring states are used, except for the spin projection component of the J/ψ equal to zero, as noted above. In addition a coherently added background term, distributed uniformly in phase space, is introduced.
7 . 3 first validation with a simple model
101
The parameters of the helicity intensity chosen for the data generation are displayed in table 7 . Here the values for the masses and widths of the resonances are taken from the Particle Data Group (PDG) [ 9 ]. In total 600 independent data samples, each with 20000 events, were generated with the the hit-or-miss MC method. For the normalization of the amplitudes in the log-likelihood of the fit, independent phase-space MC data samples with ten times more events are used.
Table 7 : Parameters of the simple model for the reaction J/ψ → γπ 0 π 0 including f 0 , f 2 as intermediate resonances. For the masses and widths of the intermediate resonances the PDG values are used [ 9 ].
Each sample is fitted 7 times with random start values for the fit parameters listed above. The masses and widths are chosen at random from a [-20 , 20 ] % interval around their PDG values. Similarly the start parameters for the magnitudes and phases are random variables of the uniform distributions ranging from [ 0 , 5 ] and [-π , π ] respectively. The coherent phase space magnitude was limited to [ 0 , 0 . 1 ] . As denoted in table 7 the λ = 0 component of the f 2 wave was chosen to be fixed in the fits. This is allowed and needed to stabilize the fitting procedure as explained in the previous chapter. For each data sample only the best fit, based on the likelihood value, was selected and used further. This procedure increases the probability of having found the global minimum.
At first the kinematic distributions of the generated datasets and their fit results can be compared. For this, one of the 600 samples with its best fit result was chosen at random. To visualize the helicity intensity of this fit result another data sample was produced using the weighted MC method. A good overview of the goodness-of-fit is given by the Dalitz plot comparison, which is shown in figure 66 2 .
From the Dalitz plot of the input data (hit-or-miss MC), the two resonances in the π 0 π 0 subsystem can be seen nicely. This is indicated by the two bands at around 1 . 7 GeV 2 /c 4 and 4 GeV 2 /c 4 . Also their spin properties can be identified when comparing the distri- bution along the bands with figures 62 and 64 . While the f 0 state at a higher mass shows no modulation, which is compatible with a spin 0 particle, the f 2 state at the lower mass resembles the angular distribution for a spin 2 particle with λ = 0 . This can be seen from the peaking at the phase space boundaries. However in this case a more distinct bump in the center of the f 2 band should be present. This in turn is explained by the destructive interference of the λ = 0 and λ = 2 waves of the f 2 , which is supported nicely by the parameter values given in table 7 .
2 Refer to appendix C. 1 for basic information about the kinematics of a Dalitz plot

To balance speed and performance, a multi-layered selection strategy is adopted. Rather than treating the STT as a uniform cloud of hits, the algorithm analyzes the hit distribution row by row. To maximize the geometric lever arm for curvature determination, the hits are categorized into inner, mid, and outer rows based on their radial position. The algorithm prioritizes triplets formed by selecting one hit from each of these distinct regions (Inner → Mid → Outer). This long-baseline selection ensures that the triplet spans the maximum available track length, resulting in a stable and precise circle fit. Within this radial framework, a further reduction of candidates is achieved using a strategy inspired by Cellular Automata. The detector is segmented into angular sectors in 𝜑 , and spatially adjacent STT hits that form a continuous chain are grouped into segments. The search for triplet partners is then restricted to hits that are both topologically connected and 𝜑 -compatible. Specifically, the second and third hits must be reachable via the neighbor map, ensuring that the combination follows the particle's path through the straw tubes. In addition, the hits are required to lie within a compatible angular range in 𝜑 , thereby rejecting combinations that would imply unphysical 'zig-zag' trajectories.
Reconstruction Strategy
121
This two-tiered approach-first defining the radial strategy (Inner/Mid/Outer) to ensure quality, then using neighbor connectivity to ensure speed-allows the Apollonius tracker finder to reconstruct displaced tracks with high efficiency while keeping the computing time manageable.
Solving the Apollonius Problem Once a valid triplet is formed by selecting one hit from each of the distinct radial groups (Inner, Mid, and Outer rows), it serves as a geometric seed. The algorithm then proceeds to determine the full track parameters through a 'Hypothesis and Test' approach.
Step 1: Calculation of Candidate Trajectories. The three selected drift circles define a classical Problem of Apollonius. From a mathematical standpoint, up to eight distinct circles can be constructed that are simultaneously tangent to three given circles, corresponding to the different combinations of internal and external tangency. The algorithm analytically computes the parameters ( 𝑥 𝑐 , 𝑦 𝑐 , 𝑅 ) for all eight solutions. Each of these solutions represents a track hypothesis, reflecting the possible particle trajectories arising from the left-right ambiguities of the drift tube measurements.
Step 2: Hit Assignment (Track Growing). To identify which of these hypotheses corresponds to a physical particle, the algorithm validates each candidate against the full set of available STT hits. For every Apollonius circle, a search is performed over the axial hits, and a hit is assigned to the candidate if its measured drift distance is consistent with the circle trajectory within a predefined tolerance. Through this procedure, the purely mathematical solutions are transformed into populated track candidates.
Step 3: Selection of the Proper Circle. The final step is the selection of the proper physical trajectory among the populated candidates. This choice is based on a composite quality metric that combines topological, statistical, and geometric considerations. First, the algorithm checks the continuity of the assigned hits, requiring that they form a topologically connected and nearly gap-free chain along the straw tubes; candidates that produce fragmented or discontinuous segments are rejected. Among the remaining solutions, preference is given to the candidate that associates the largest number of hits, as a trajectory supported by more measurements is statistically more robust than one constrained only by the initial triplet.

The PandaRoot framework incorporates a modular design approach, where each subsystem is allocated its own package for Monte Carlo processing, digitization, reconstruction, tracking and particle identification (PID). The detector components within each subsystem employ unique algorithms to compute the probability density function (PDF) for each particle hypothesis. The combination of the PDFs from all detector components is accomplished through the use of a Bayesian approach, resulting in a global likelihood for PID.
Upon completion of data flow, the PandaRoot framework offers a range of algorithms for the tracking and particle identification, in addition to comprehensive analysis tools including the 𝑅ℎ𝑜 package and the kinematic fitter package. The latter package facilitates a range of fitting techniques, including vertex fitting, mass constraint fitting, 4C Kinematic fitting, and decay tree fitting. The Rho package provides a unique mechanism for consolidating particle candidate lists, which effectively eliminates the potential for double counting through the use of indexed candidates. Additionally, the package includes support for PID, tracking, and generated Monte Carlo information, further enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of the physics analysis process.

### 3.2 Displaced-track reconstruction

Standard primary-track finders often assume that tracks originate close to the nominal beam axis. This is inappropriate for Restgas interactions distributed over a long region.

The dedicated reconstruction chain is configured in:

- `macro/target/reco_complete.C`

Its relevant stages are:

1. `PndTrkTracking2` performs the standard reconstruction.
2. `PndUnassignedHitsTask` collects hits not assigned by the standard track finder.
3. `PndApolloniusTripletTrackFinderTask` reconstructs displaced trajectories using STT drift-circle triplets and MVD/GEM information.
4. `PndSttSkewStrawPzFinderTask` recovers the longitudinal track component from skewed STT layers.
5. `PndRecoKalmanTask2` fits the resulting tracks with `SetPropagateToIP(kFALSE)`.

The workflow initiates with the processing of experimental data. The raw hits from the STT are first utilized by the Apollonius algorithm to generate initial track seeds, which are subsequently refined by the Kalman Filter with hits from MVD and GEM to produce fitted trajectories. Following the tracking stage, a first PID step is performed. At this intermediate stage, the PID step is executed without specific back-propagation, utilizing standard assumptions to provide an initial particle hypotheses. These preliminary tracks are then paired to analytically calculate the geometric POCA, providing the first reliable 3D estimate of the event vertex.

Reconstruction Strategy
123
Integration with MVD and GEM (Global Tracking)
The output of the combined Apollonius and Pz Finder stages is a track seed based solely on STT information. While this seed is highly effective for identifying displaced tracks, it does not yet provide the precision required for accurate vertex reconstruction. The full integration of information from all tracking sub-detectors is therefore performed in the final Kalman filtering stage.
The Apollonius algorithm supplies an initial track candidate derived from STT isochrones, which defines a preliminary trajectory but does not include the highprecision measurements from the silicon-based detectors. These track candidates are subsequently processed by the KalmanFit using the GenFit framework, which applies a statistically rigorous Kalman filter to combine measurements from different detector systems. During this procedure, the STT-based helix is extrapolated inward toward the MVD volume, where compatible pixel or strip hits are searched for and, if found, incorporated into the track. This inward propagation significantly improves the resolution of the impact parameters 𝑑 0 and 𝑧 0 and is crucial for precisely locating the interaction vertex. In parallel, the track is extrapolated outward to the GEM stations, where additional measurements refine the momentum determination, particularly for forward-going particles, leading to an improved relative momentum resolution 𝑑𝑝/𝑝 .
As a result, the final reconstructed tracks coherently combine information from all tracking subsystems-MVD, STT, and GEM-leveraging the large acceptance and pattern recognition capability of the STT together with the superior spatial resolution of the MVD and GEM to achieve precise vertex and momentum reconstruction.
PID Step
The accurate determination of particle kinematics relies not only on precise track fitting but also on the correct association of reconstructed tracks with their physical interaction vertex during the PID step. Track candidates produced by the track finder are represented as infinite helices extending throughout the detector volume. Consequently, a crucial task of the PID step is the determination of the true physical origin of these trajectories, in order to effectively anchor and terminate them at their source. Without a well-defined starting point, essential kinematic quantities-most notably the momentum vector and the path length required for energy-loss corrections-cannot be uniquely or reliably determined.
This issue becomes particularly severe in the presence of Restgas background, where interactions occur at arbitrary locations along and within the beam pipe rather than being confined to the nominal target region. Under these conditions, the IP determination approach in the PID step must be reconsidered.
Limitations of the Standard Approach: In the standard PandaRoot workflow, a strong geometric constraint is imposed by assuming that particle trajectories originate from the beam axis near the nominal interaction point. As a result, tracks identified by the finder are processed by a Kalman Filter and typically propagated forward by ≈ 2 cm, then Kalman-fitted tracks are propagated to the point of closest approach to the 𝑧 -axis (POCA-to-line), which is then used to define the reference momentum vector and path length for the PID step.

Limitations of the Standard Approach: In the standard PandaRoot workflow, a strong geometric constraint is imposed by assuming that particle trajectories originate from the beam axis near the nominal interaction point. As a result, tracks identified by the finder are processed by a Kalman Filter and typically propagated forward by ≈ 2 cm, then Kalman-fitted tracks are propagated to the point of closest approach to the 𝑧 -axis (POCA-to-line), which is then used to define the reference momentum vector and path length for the PID step.
124
Precise Measurement of the Restgas Distribution
While this approximation is well justified for interactions localized within the target region, it leads to significant systematic biases when applied to interactions with Restgas particles. Owing to the beam complication and the extended longitudinal density profile of the Restgas background, such interactions are distributed stochastically along the vacuum pipe and may exhibit substantial displacements in both transverse ( 𝑥, 𝑦 ) and longitudinal ( 𝑧 ) directions. Forcing a helical trajectory to reference the beam axis when its true origin is displaced by several centimeters can result in severe reconstruction distortions. In particular, transverse offsets may cause the geometric solver to fail or produce ambiguous solutions, while longitudinal displacements lead to an incorrect estimation of the particle's flight path through the detector material. This path-length miscalculation directly affects the energyloss ( 𝑑𝐸/𝑑𝑥 ) correction and introduces a systematic bias in the reconstructed polar angle 𝜃 , as the momentum vector is effectively evaluated at an unphysical reference plane.
Modified POCA-First Approach: To address these topological limitations, a modified reconstruction scheme, referred to as the POCA-First Approach , was developed. Starting from the global track candidates seeded by the Apollonius finder and produced by the Kalman filter, the algorithm analytically computes the threedimensional point of closest approach (POCA) of all the tracks of the elastically scattered ¯ 𝑝𝑝 events. The resulting coordinate, ⃗ 𝑣 POCA , provides an estimator of the true interaction vertex and serves as the physical anchor point for subsequent kinematic reconstruction.
Once the geometric vertex ⃗ 𝑣 POCA is established, the Kalman-fitted tracks perform a targeted back-propagation. The track parameters are propagated from the outer detectors back specifically to the point of closest approach, to the 3D coordinate ⃗ 𝑣 POCA (POCA-to-point), rather than to the 𝑧 -axis. This POCA-to-point back-propagation effectively reconstructs the IP for displaced vertices, ensuring that the track parameters are evaluated at the actual interaction location. It is at this location that the momentum vector is evaluated, and the path length is determined for the energy loss calculation. This ensures that the PID algorithms receive kinematic inputs that correctly reflect the particle's history through the detector material and magnetic field up to the actual point of interaction.
By anchoring the track parameters to the reconstructed interaction vertex rather than an arbitrary axis, this approach effectively eliminates the systematic biases introduced by displaced vertices, thereby enabling accurate IP and momentum reconstruction and particle identification for events from beam-Restgas interactions. The validity of using this calculated geometric estimator was rigorously verified through simulation studies.

This section details the modifications implemented in the PandaRoot framework to achieve precise track reconstruction and particle identification for events originating away from the nominal IP.
The analysis presented in this work is based on the PandaRoot framework, version oct19 . This specific release was selected to ensure the stability of the tracking algorithms. Newer iterations of the framework were found to exhibit regressions in the primary track reconstruction quality even for standard events at the origin, necessitating the use of the robust oct19 release as the baseline for this study.
Tracking for Displaced Vertices: The Apollonius Algorithm
The first stage of track reconstruction is the track finding. The standard tracking algorithms in PANDA (e.g., the Barrel Track Finder) generally optimize performance by imposing a constraint that tracks must originate from the primary vertex region ( 𝑥 ≈ 𝑦 ≈ 0). While effective for the nominal IP, this assumption leads to inefficiencies and systematic biases when reconstructing tracks from displaced vertices, such as those arising from interactions with Restgas particles or shifted beam-target collisions.
In the case of interactions with Restgas particles, the reaction vertices are distributed along the beam axis ( 𝑧 ) and can exhibit transverse offsets. To recover these displaced tracks, which topologically resemble secondary decay products, a track finder developed for secondary vertices called Apollonius Triplet Track Finder was integrated into the reconstruction chain [147, 148].
The reconstruction of displaced tracks is implemented as a two-stage process within the PandaRoot framework. The first stage performs pattern recognition in the 𝑥𝑦 -plane using the axial STT layers. The second stage recovers the longitudinal ( 𝑧 ) information using the skewed STT layers.
The algorithm is mathematically grounded in the classical Problem of Apollonius (circa 200 BC), which seeks to construct a circle that is tangent to three given circles. Unlike global Hough transforms, this algorithm constructs tracks locally from triplets of hits. The implementation of the algorithm within the PandaRoot framework addresses two main computational challenges: the combinatorial selection of hits and the ambiguity of the geometric solution.
Triplet Selection Strategy The first step of the algorithm, selecting three STT hits ( ℎ 1 , ℎ 2 , ℎ 3 ) to form a triplet, is critical. A brute-force combination of all available hits would result in an unmanageable combinatorial explosion. Conversely, if the selection criteria are too tight, valid tracks might be discarded, leading to a drop in efficiency.

# RestgasDetermination

A PandaRoot-based research branch for reconstructing and correcting the longitudinal residual-gas (“Restgas”) interaction profile in the PANDA target region.

This repository is based on the PandaRoot `oct19` tag. The Restgas-specific development starts after commit `ef9a564`. The principal analysis code is located in [`macro/target`](macro/target). This document describes the current `oct19` workflow, including the event-by-event POCA hand-off, configurable beam momentum and Restgas profile, and profile-dependent efficiency correction.

> **Scope and maturity**
>
> The current repository is a **Monte Carlo research implementation used for the studies in Chapters 7 and 8 of the associated thesis**. It contains the main ingredients of the Restgas-determination method, including distributed target generation, displaced-track reconstruction, POCA-based back-propagation, vertex reconstruction, and profile-dependent efficiency correction.
>
> The analysis and correction macros are designed primarily for Monte Carlo closure, efficiency, and systematic studies corresponding to the thesis workflow.

To constrain this dominant systematic uncertainty, the investigation extended beyond software algorithms to evaluate the feasibility of a hardware-driven solution utilizing the tracking system. The study proposed the upgrade of the Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS), leveraging technology originally developed for the Luminosity Detector itself. It was demonstrated that the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS, thinned to just 50 𝜇 m, minimizes the multiple Coulomb scattering that typically degrades tracking performance at low momenta. Coupled with a fine pixel pitch of 80 × 80 𝜇 m 2 , this hardware configuration achieves a longitudinal vertex resolution of approximately 20 𝜇 m, providing the necessary sensitivity to resolve the Restgas distribution which is inaccessible to the Luminosity Detector alone. To fully exploit this hardware potential, a specialized reconstruction chain was implemented, utilizing the Apollonius triplet finder for off-IP tracking and a 'POCA-to-Point' back-propagation algorithm. This strategy optimized the reconstruction efficiency for events originating away from the nominal interaction point, allowing for the recovery of the physical density profile via a robust one-dimensional efficiency correction.
144
Summary and Outlook
The culmination of this work is the integration of the measured Restgas profile back into the luminosity determination chain, establishing a self-consistent analysis cycle. Through the implementation of a profile-dependent efficiency correction and a robust iterative workflow, the target profile with Restgas background is successfully reconstructed without the reliance on the initial model. The reconstructed profile is then used to generate an 'Effective Acceptance Map' for the luminosity fit, effectively suppressing the systematic uncertainty associated with the target profile with Restgas background to better than 0.5%. By proving that the Restgas distribution can be precisely reconstructed and accounted for, this research ensures that the deviation in the luminosity determination will not limit the PANDA experiment's ability to map the exotic hadron spectrum, thereby fulfilling the rigorous demands of next-generation hadron physics.

Determination of the Restgas Profile
Building upon the reconstruction algorithms established in Chapter 7, specifically the Apollonius tracking and the POCA-based vertexing, this chapter evaluates the final performance of the Restgas profile measurement. The primary objective is to extract the longitudinal density distribution, 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ), from the reconstructed event rate. This process requires a rigorous handling of detector acceptance limits and, crucially, the correction of resolution effects arising from the extreme density gradients between the target and the Restgas background.
8.1 Definition of the Measurement Range
Unlike conventional analyses that focus solely on the immediate vicinity of the Interaction Point (IP), the Restgas determination requires a global perspective along the entire beam axis. The measurement range is explicitly defined as 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m, a decision driven by the physical constraints of the PANDA vacuum system and the tracking detector layout. The upstream limit at 𝑧 = -3 . 0 m is determined by the location of the powerful cryogenic pump system in the beam line. As illustrated in the vacuum profile simulation (Figure 3.14), the Restgas density drops by several orders of magnitude beyond this point due to the effective pumping, rendering the gas contribution physically negligible. Similarly, the downstream boundary at 𝑧 = +6 . 0 m is constrained by the geometrical acceptance of the Forward Tracker (FT), which features its last two layers at 𝑧 = 6075mm and 𝑧 = 6545mm. Tracks originating significantly beyond this point cannot produce sufficient hits to form reconstructible candidates. Crucially, the vacuum distribution studies indicate that this defined region contains more than 99% of the total integrated Restgas density. Consequently, the distribution measured within this global range effectively represents the complete Restgas profile required for the luminosity determination, thereby eliminating the need for model-dependent extrapolations outside the detector acceptance.

The studies in Section 5.4 have clearly demonstrated the necessity of a precise measurement of the target distribution along the beam axis. Furthermore, the simulation studies in Section 6.3 have established that the upgraded MVD with HV-MAPS technology provides the necessary hardware performance, specifically the excellent spatial resolution and low material budget, to resolve the longitudinal distribution of Restgas background. However, the hardware upgrade alone is insufficient to extract the Restgas profile with the precision required for luminosity determination. To achieve this, the precise measurement of the longitudinal target profile will be performed specifically utilizing antiproton-proton (¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) elastic scattering events, which serve as a high-statistics and kinematically well-understood reference channel.
A fundamental challenge lies in the event reconstruction algorithms. The standard reconstruction chain in the PandaRoot framework is primarily optimized for physics channels originating from the nominal IP at (0 , 0 , 0). Beam-Restgas interactions, however, are distributed along the entire beam axis, often extending centimeters or decimeters away from the IP. Applying standard tracking and particle identification (PID) routines to these displaced vertices introduces systematic biases, as track parameters and error matrices are typically propagated to the origin rather than the true interaction vertex. To overcome this limitation, a dedicated reconstruction algorithm tailored for shifted IP scenarios is essential. This algorithm must accurately account for the spatial distribution of the beam-Restgas interactions, ensuring that track fitting and vertex reconstruction are performed with respect to the actual interaction points rather than the nominal IP.

The accurate reconstruction of the interaction vertex distribution of the elastically scattered ¯ 𝑝𝑝 events which also originate by interactions of beam particles with Restgas profiles necessitates specialized algorithms capable of handling displaced vertices.

The capability of the PANDA detector, specifically the upgraded Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) utilizing HVMAPS technology has been established, to perform a precise, data-driven measurement of the Restgas density profile over the full range of 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m. The superior vertexing resolution and reduced material budget of the sensors are critical factors that enable the effective determination of the Restgas distribution even for interactions significantly displaced from the nominal IP.
Through the implementation of a profile-dependent efficiency correction and a robust iterative workflow, the systematic distortions caused by resolution smearing and initial model inaccuracies are rigorously suppressed. This method acts as a contracting map, converging to the true physical distribution and ensuring that the final result is independent of the initial simulation input provided by the Target Group. To quantify the stability of this approach, an iterative procedure was initialized with an extreme starting condition: a 40% overestimation of the Restgas distribution. As summarized in Table 9.1, the iterative procedure converges rapidly. Within merely three steps, the global deviation drops from 12 . 27% to 1 . 30%, and the deviation in the central region vanishes to -0 . 22%. Consequently, the precise density profile can be derived directly from the experimental data across the entire relevant domain, providing the reliable input essential for the absolute luminosity determination.
Finally, the determined Restgas profile was integrated back into the LuminosityFit framework to validate the complete analysis chain. The luminosity determination was performed at a beam momentum of 𝑝 𝑏𝑒𝑎𝑚 = 4 . 06 GeV /𝑐 , applying a cut within the analysis window ( | 𝑥 | , | 𝑦 | < 1 cm and | 𝑧 | < 5 cm). The relative deviation of the determined luminosity (Δ ℒ / ℒ ) is (0 . 05 ± 0 . 07)% with the reconstructed target profile with Restgas background. As presented in Table 9.2, this result is consistent with the ideal case where the target is treated as point-like and the efficiency correction is based on a point-like model, which yields a deviation of -0 . 036 ± 0 . 07% and also with the case where the target profile with Restgas background is well-known and totally the same as real data, which yields a deviation of 0 . 02 ± 0 . 08%. This results demonstrate that the synergy of high-precision tracking and advanced fitting algorithms transforms the Restgas background from a limiting systematic background into a precisely monitored observable, enabling a robust and accurate luminosity determination for the PANDA experiment.

For the LMD analysis, the Cellular Automaton algorithm is the preferred choice [92]. The implementation used in this work creates track candidates requiring hits in at least 3 out of 4 stations to ensure high efficiency while suppressing ghost tracks.
Track Fitting with GenFit
Once track candidates are found, their kinematic parameters must be estimated. The reconstruction utilizes the GenFit toolkit [130], which supports multiple fitting algorithms, most notably the General Broken Lines (GBL) [131, 132] fit and the Kalman Filter [133, 134].
General Broken Lines (GBL) The GBL algorithm constructs a trajectory from a sequence of thin scatterers. It is particularly powerful for detector alignment as it provides explicit access to the residuals of all measurements simultaneously.
Kalman Filter The Kalman filter is a recursive estimator that updates the track state vector ⃗ 𝑞 = ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧, 𝑝 𝑥 , 𝑝 𝑦 , 𝑝 𝑧 ) at each measurement plane. It is the preferred algorithm for track reconstruction due to its superior handling of complex material effects. Specifically, it incorporates deterministic energy dissipation governed by the Bethe-Bloch formula when particles traverse the detector sensors and support structures. Furthermore, the filter elegantly accounts for Multiple Coulomb Scattering (MCS) by treating it as stochastic process noise. This approach appropriately inflates the track's covariance matrix, accurately reflecting the accumulated spatial uncertainties induced by the detector's material budget.
For the determination of the luminosity, the Kalman Filter is selected as the primary fitting algorithm. This ensures that the final error estimates at the first detector layer are statistically rigorous, which is a prerequisite for the accurate back-propagation to the interaction point.
Back-Propagation to the Interaction Point
For luminosity determination, the physics observable is the scattering angle 𝜃 at the Interaction Point ( 𝑧 = 0), not at the detector ( 𝑧 ≈ 11 m). Between the IP and the LMD, the antiprotons traverse the stray field of the solenoid and the strong dipole magnet field, which deflects trajectories horizontally. To recover the true scattering angle, the fitted tracks must be propagated backwards using the GEANE track propagator [135, 136]. This step involves a subtle but critical assumption regarding the particle momentum.

### 3.2 Displaced-track reconstruction

Standard primary-track finders often assume that tracks originate close to the nominal beam axis. This is inappropriate for Restgas interactions distributed over a long region.

The dedicated reconstruction chain is configured in:

- `macro/target/reco_complete.C`

Its relevant stages are:

1. `PndTrkTracking2` performs the standard reconstruction.
2. `PndUnassignedHitsTask` collects hits not assigned by the standard track finder.
3. `PndApolloniusTripletTrackFinderTask` reconstructs displaced trajectories using STT drift-circle triplets and MVD/GEM information.
4. `PndSttSkewStrawPzFinderTask` recovers the longitudinal track component from skewed STT layers.

For candidates with comparable hit counts, the geometric fit quality is evaluated by computing the quadratic distance of the assigned hits to the candidate circle,
where 𝑑 𝑖 denotes the distance from the center of the 𝑖 -th hit to the track center and 𝑅 is the track radius. The solution that minimizes this quantity, corresponding to the best overall geometric consistency, is selected as the final track seed. This robust selection procedure ensures that the algorithm does not merely identify a mathematical circle passing through three points, but reconstructs a physically meaningful trajectory that is supported by the maximum amount of detector information.
Longitudinal Reconstruction (Skewed Straw Pz Finder)
The two-dimensional circles obtained from the Apollonius step fully define the track curvature in the 𝑥𝑦 -plane, but they do not provide any information on the longitudinal coordinate 𝑧 . The reconstruction of the third dimension is therefore performed in a subsequent step by the Pz Finder, which exploits the specific geometry of the skewed STT layers that are tilted by ± 2 . 9 ∘ with respect to the beam axis.
Starting from the two-dimensional track candidates, the algorithm searches for hits in the skewed straw layers that are geometrically compatible with the extrapolated 2D circle. Once such hits are identified, the intersection between the cylindrical surface defined by the 2D track and the corresponding skewed straw wire which is modeled as a straight line in three-dimensional space is calculated. Owing to the stereo angle 𝛼 of the skewed layers, the position of this intersection along the wire is directly correlated with the longitudinal position of the track. The 𝑧 -coordinate of each intersection point is obtained according to
where 𝜑 int denotes the azimuthal angle of the intersection and 𝑅 is the track radius, 𝛼 is the aforementioned stereo angle defining the wire inclination, and 𝑧 0 represents the longitudinal offset of the track (i.e., its 𝑧 -coordinate at the reference azimuth 𝜑 = 0).
By accumulating multiple measurements from different skewed layers, the algorithm performs a linear regression in the 𝑠 -𝑧 plane, with 𝑠 = 𝑅𝜑 representing the arc length along the track. The slope of this fit determines the dip angle 𝜆 and, consequently, the longitudinal momentum component 𝑝 𝑧 , while the intercept yields the 𝑧 -position of the track origin. By decoupling the pattern recognition in the transverse plane from the longitudinal reconstruction, this method enables the efficient reconstruction of tracks with arbitrary production points, making it particularly well suited for recovering Restgas events distributed along the beam axis.

Reconstruction Strategy
123
Integration with MVD and GEM (Global Tracking)
The output of the combined Apollonius and Pz Finder stages is a track seed based solely on STT information. While this seed is highly effective for identifying displaced tracks, it does not yet provide the precision required for accurate vertex reconstruction. The full integration of information from all tracking sub-detectors is therefore performed in the final Kalman filtering stage.
The Apollonius algorithm supplies an initial track candidate derived from STT isochrones, which defines a preliminary trajectory but does not include the highprecision measurements from the silicon-based detectors. These track candidates are subsequently processed by the KalmanFit using the GenFit framework, which applies a statistically rigorous Kalman filter to combine measurements from different detector systems. During this procedure, the STT-based helix is extrapolated inward toward the MVD volume, where compatible pixel or strip hits are searched for and, if found, incorporated into the track. This inward propagation significantly improves the resolution of the impact parameters 𝑑 0 and 𝑧 0 and is crucial for precisely locating the interaction vertex. In parallel, the track is extrapolated outward to the GEM stations, where additional measurements refine the momentum determination, particularly for forward-going particles, leading to an improved relative momentum resolution 𝑑𝑝/𝑝 .
As a result, the final reconstructed tracks coherently combine information from all tracking subsystems-MVD, STT, and GEM-leveraging the large acceptance and pattern recognition capability of the STT together with the superior spatial resolution of the MVD and GEM to achieve precise vertex and momentum reconstruction.
PID Step
The accurate determination of particle kinematics relies not only on precise track fitting but also on the correct association of reconstructed tracks with their physical interaction vertex during the PID step. Track candidates produced by the track finder are represented as infinite helices extending throughout the detector volume. Consequently, a crucial task of the PID step is the determination of the true physical origin of these trajectories, in order to effectively anchor and terminate them at their source. Without a well-defined starting point, essential kinematic quantities-most notably the momentum vector and the path length required for energy-loss corrections-cannot be uniquely or reliably determined.
This issue becomes particularly severe in the presence of Restgas background, where interactions occur at arbitrary locations along and within the beam pipe rather than being confined to the nominal target region. Under these conditions, the IP determination approach in the PID step must be reconsidered.
Limitations of the Standard Approach: In the standard PandaRoot workflow, a strong geometric constraint is imposed by assuming that particle trajectories originate from the beam axis near the nominal interaction point. As a result, tracks identified by the finder are processed by a Kalman Filter and typically propagated forward by ≈ 2 cm, then Kalman-fitted tracks are propagated to the point of closest approach to the 𝑧 -axis (POCA-to-line), which is then used to define the reference momentum vector and path length for the PID step.

This section details the modifications implemented in the PandaRoot framework to achieve precise track reconstruction and particle identification for events originating away from the nominal IP.
The analysis presented in this work is based on the PandaRoot framework, version oct19 . This specific release was selected to ensure the stability of the tracking algorithms. Newer iterations of the framework were found to exhibit regressions in the primary track reconstruction quality even for standard events at the origin, necessitating the use of the robust oct19 release as the baseline for this study.
Tracking for Displaced Vertices: The Apollonius Algorithm
The first stage of track reconstruction is the track finding. The standard tracking algorithms in PANDA (e.g., the Barrel Track Finder) generally optimize performance by imposing a constraint that tracks must originate from the primary vertex region ( 𝑥 ≈ 𝑦 ≈ 0). While effective for the nominal IP, this assumption leads to inefficiencies and systematic biases when reconstructing tracks from displaced vertices, such as those arising from interactions with Restgas particles or shifted beam-target collisions.
In the case of interactions with Restgas particles, the reaction vertices are distributed along the beam axis ( 𝑧 ) and can exhibit transverse offsets. To recover these displaced tracks, which topologically resemble secondary decay products, a track finder developed for secondary vertices called Apollonius Triplet Track Finder was integrated into the reconstruction chain [147, 148].
The reconstruction of displaced tracks is implemented as a two-stage process within the PandaRoot framework. The first stage performs pattern recognition in the 𝑥𝑦 -plane using the axial STT layers. The second stage recovers the longitudinal ( 𝑧 ) information using the skewed STT layers.
The algorithm is mathematically grounded in the classical Problem of Apollonius (circa 200 BC), which seeks to construct a circle that is tangent to three given circles. Unlike global Hough transforms, this algorithm constructs tracks locally from triplets of hits. The implementation of the algorithm within the PandaRoot framework addresses two main computational challenges: the combinatorial selection of hits and the ambiguity of the geometric solution.
Triplet Selection Strategy The first step of the algorithm, selecting three STT hits ( ℎ 1 , ℎ 2 , ℎ 3 ) to form a triplet, is critical. A brute-force combination of all available hits would result in an unmanageable combinatorial explosion. Conversely, if the selection criteria are too tight, valid tracks might be discarded, leading to a drop in efficiency.

The results of this dependency study are summarized in Figure 7.6. The analysis reveals a dramatic variation in efficiency along the beam axis ( 𝑧 ). As the interaction point shifts away from the detector center, the efficiency drops precipitously from a maximum of ∼ 81% at 𝑧 = 0cm to approximately 6% at the downstream edge 𝑧 = 10cm, primarily due to the acceptance coverage of the PANDA Target Spectrometer. In strong contrast, the efficiency remains remarkably stable with respect to transverse displacements. Within the central core region ( | 𝑥 | , | 𝑦 | < 0 . 5 cm), the variation in efficiency is negligible. Considering that the transverse profile of the real beam-Restgas interaction is tightly constrained by the beam emittance (typically well within the ± 0 . 5 cm window), the transverse efficiency uniformity holds true for the experimental conditions.
Consequently, this study concludes that the transverse dependence can be safely neglected. A 1D longitudinal efficiency curve 𝜀 ( 𝑧 ) provides a sufficient and robust model for the correction of the reconstructed data. This finding allows for the precise recovery of the Restgas distribution by simply weighting the reconstructed 𝑧 -spectrum by the inverse of the z-dependent efficiency, significantly simplifying the analysis framework without compromising physical accuracy.

With the implementation of the Apollonius triplet track finder and the POCA-First PID approach, the full reconstruction chain is established. This section validates the effectiveness of this workflow using Monte Carlo simulations and presents the final results for the Restgas profile determination.

To rigorously verify this, a simulation study was performed using 10,000 ¯ 𝑝𝑝 elastic scattering events generated by the DPM generator at a beam momentum of 𝑝 beam = 4 . 06 GeV /𝑐 . Geometric Accuracy: The distribution of the reconstructed POCA vertex for each event was analyzed to assess the intrinsic resolution of the tracking system without a back-propagation constraint. As shown in Figure 7.1, the POCA vertex yields a distribution centered near the true value with a finite spread due to tracking uncertainties. Limitations of the Standard Approach: In the standard PandaRoot workflow, a strong geometric constraint is imposed by assuming that particle trajectories originate from the beam axis near the nominal interaction point. As a result, tracks identified by the finder are processed by a Kalman Filter and typically propagated forward by ≈ 2 cm, then Kalman-fitted tracks are propagated to the point of closest approach to the 𝑧 -axis (POCA-to-line), which is then used to define the reference momentum vector and path length for the PID step.
124
Precise Measurement of the Restgas Distribution
While this approximation is well justified for interactions localized within the target region, it leads to significant systematic biases when applied to interactions with Restgas particles. Owing to the beam complication and the extended longitudinal density profile of the Restgas background, such interactions are distributed stochastically along the vacuum pipe and may exhibit substantial displacements in both transverse ( 𝑥, 𝑦 ) and longitudinal ( 𝑧 ) directions. Forcing a helical trajectory to reference the beam axis when its true origin is displaced by several centimeters can result in severe reconstruction distortions. In particular, transverse offsets may cause the geometric solver to fail or produce ambiguous solutions, while longitudinal displacements lead to an incorrect estimation of the particle's flight path through the detector material. This path-length miscalculation directly affects the energyloss ( 𝑑𝐸/𝑑𝑥 ) correction and introduces a systematic bias in the reconstructed polar angle 𝜃 , as the momentum vector is effectively evaluated at an unphysical reference plane.
Modified POCA-First Approach: To address these topological limitations, a modified reconstruction scheme, referred to as the POCA-First Approach , was developed. Starting from the global track candidates seeded by the Apollonius finder and produced by the Kalman filter, the algorithm analytically computes the threedimensional point of closest approach (POCA) of all the tracks of the elastically scattered ¯ 𝑝𝑝 events. The resulting coordinate, ⃗ 𝑣 POCA , provides an estimator of the true interaction vertex and serves as the physical anchor point for subsequent kinematic reconstruction.
Once the geometric vertex ⃗ 𝑣 POCA is established, the Kalman-fitted tracks perform a targeted back-propagation. The track parameters are propagated from the outer detectors back specifically to the point of closest approach, to the 3D coordinate ⃗ 𝑣 POCA (POCA-to-point), rather than to the 𝑧 -axis. This POCA-to-point back-propagation effectively reconstructs the IP for displaced vertices, ensuring that the track parameters are evaluated at the actual interaction location. It is at this location that the momentum vector is evaluated, and the path length is determined for the energy loss calculation. This ensures that the PID algorithms receive kinematic inputs that correctly reflect the particle's history through the detector material and magnetic field up to the actual point of interaction.
By anchoring the track parameters to the reconstructed interaction vertex rather than an arbitrary axis, this approach effectively eliminates the systematic biases introduced by displaced vertices, thereby enabling accurate IP and momentum reconstruction and particle identification for events from beam-Restgas interactions. The validity of using this calculated geometric estimator was rigorously verified through simulation studies.

Chapter8
Determination of the Restgas Profile
Building upon the reconstruction algorithms established in Chapter 7, specifically the Apollonius tracking and the POCA-based vertexing, this chapter evaluates the final performance of the Restgas profile measurement. The primary objective is to extract the longitudinal density distribution, 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ), from the reconstructed event rate. This process requires a rigorous handling of detector acceptance limits and, crucially, the correction of resolution effects arising from the extreme density gradients between the target and the Restgas background.
8.1 Definition of the Measurement Range
Unlike conventional analyses that focus solely on the immediate vicinity of the Interaction Point (IP), the Restgas determination requires a global perspective along the entire beam axis. The measurement range is explicitly defined as 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m, a decision driven by the physical constraints of the PANDA vacuum system and the tracking detector layout. The upstream limit at 𝑧 = -3 . 0 m is determined by the location of the powerful cryogenic pump system in the beam line. As illustrated in the vacuum profile simulation (Figure 3.14), the Restgas density drops by several orders of magnitude beyond this point due to the effective pumping, rendering the gas contribution physically negligible. Similarly, the downstream boundary at 𝑧 = +6 . 0 m is constrained by the geometrical acceptance of the Forward Tracker (FT), which features its last two layers at 𝑧 = 6075mm and 𝑧 = 6545mm. Tracks originating significantly beyond this point cannot produce sufficient hits to form reconstructible candidates. Crucially, the vacuum distribution studies indicate that this defined region contains more than 99% of the total integrated Restgas density. Consequently, the distribution measured within this global range effectively represents the complete Restgas profile required for the luminosity determination, thereby eliminating the need for model-dependent extrapolations outside the detector acceptance.

To constrain this dominant systematic uncertainty, the investigation extended beyond software algorithms to evaluate the feasibility of a hardware-driven solution utilizing the tracking system. The study proposed the upgrade of the Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS), leveraging technology originally developed for the Luminosity Detector itself. It was demonstrated that the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS, thinned to just 50 𝜇 m, minimizes the multiple Coulomb scattering that typically degrades tracking performance at low momenta. Coupled with a fine pixel pitch of 80 × 80 𝜇 m 2 , this hardware configuration achieves a longitudinal vertex resolution of approximately 20 𝜇 m, providing the necessary sensitivity to resolve the Restgas distribution which is inaccessible to the Luminosity Detector alone. To fully exploit this hardware potential, a specialized reconstruction chain was implemented, utilizing the Apollonius triplet finder for off-IP tracking and a 'POCA-to-Point' back-propagation algorithm. This strategy optimized the reconstruction efficiency for events originating away from the nominal interaction point, allowing for the recovery of the physical density profile via a robust one-dimensional efficiency correction.

Summary and Outlook
The culmination of this work is the integration of the measured Restgas profile back into the luminosity determination chain, establishing a self-consistent analysis cycle. Through the implementation of a profile-dependent efficiency correction and a robust iterative workflow, the target profile with Restgas background is successfully reconstructed without the reliance on the initial model. The reconstructed profile is then used to generate an 'Effective Acceptance Map' for the luminosity fit, effectively suppressing the systematic uncertainty associated with the target profile with Restgas background to better than 0.5%. By proving that the Restgas distribution can be precisely reconstructed and accounted for, this research ensures that the deviation in the luminosity determination will not limit the PANDA experiment's ability to map the exotic hadron spectrum, thereby fulfilling the rigorous demands of next-generation hadron physics.

Summary and Outlook
The PANDA experiment at the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) represents the future precision frontier of hadron physics, addressing fundamental questions regarding the strong interaction, including the search for gluonic excitations, the spectroscopy of charmonium states, and the investigation of nucleon structure. A prerequisite for fully exploiting this discovery potential-particularly for the measurement of absolute cross-sections and the scanning of narrow resonance lineshapes-is the precise determination of the time-integrated luminosity. While the primary luminosity measurement relies on the detection of antiproton-proton elastic scattering in the Coulomb-Nuclear Interference region, the specific conditions of the PANDA fixed-target setup introduce significant challenges that render conventional point-source approximations insufficient. Specifically, the interaction of the antiproton beam with the Restgas background distributed along the beam pipe creates a non-localized background source which, if not correctly modeled, fundamentally limits the attainable experimental precision.
To overcome these limitations, this thesis established a comprehensive methodology that transforms the handling of the extended interaction region from a systematic liability into a precisely controlled observable. Central to this approach was the refinement of the object-oriented software framework LuminosityFit , which implements a rigorous convolution model combining the theoretical differential cross-section with the detector's resolution and geometric acceptance. By incorporating a Dual Parton Model (DPM) to accurately describe the hadronic amplitude and introducing the concept of an 'Effective Acceptance Map', the framework successfully integrates the complex, smeared geometry of the beam-Restgas overlap into the fitting procedure. Extensive validation studies demonstrated that this algorithmic approach robustly decouples the luminosity signal from background contributions induced by beam systematics, effectively correcting for beam tilts, transverse offsets, and statistical divergence to recover the input luminosity with a relative statistical precision of better than 0.5%. However, sensitivity analysis revealed a critical dependency: the accuracy of the extraction is strictly bound to the prior knowledge of the longitudinal Restgas density profile. A deviation of 10% in the assumed Restgas model was shown to induce a systematic luminosity bias of approximately 3.4%, a magnitude that exceeds the stringent precision requirements necessary for the PANDA physics program.
To constrain this dominant systematic uncertainty, the investigation extended beyond software algorithms to evaluate the feasibility of a hardware-driven solution utilizing the tracking system. The study proposed the upgrade of the Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS), leveraging technology originally developed for the Luminosity Detector itself. It was demonstrated that the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS, thinned to just 50 𝜇 m, minimizes the multiple Coulomb scattering that typically degrades tracking performance at low momenta. Coupled with a fine pixel pitch of 80 × 80 𝜇 m 2 , this hardware configuration achieves a longitudinal vertex resolution of approximately 20 𝜇 m, providing the necessary sensitivity to resolve the Restgas distribution which is inaccessible to the Luminosity Detector alone. To fully exploit this hardware potential, a specialized reconstruction chain was implemented, utilizing the Apollonius triplet finder for off-IP tracking and a 'POCA-to-Point' back-propagation algorithm. Longitudinal Reconstruction (Skewed Straw Pz Finder)
The two-dimensional circles obtained from the Apollonius step fully define the track curvature in the 𝑥𝑦 -plane, but they do not provide any information on the longitudinal coordinate 𝑧 . The reconstruction of the third dimension is therefore performed in a subsequent step by the Pz Finder, which exploits the specific geometry of the skewed STT layers that are tilted by ± 2 . 9 ∘ with respect to the beam axis.
Starting from the two-dimensional track candidates, the algorithm searches for hits in the skewed straw layers that are geometrically compatible with the extrapolated 2D circle. Once such hits are identified, the intersection between the cylindrical surface defined by the 2D track and the corresponding skewed straw wire which is modeled as a straight line in three-dimensional space is calculated. Owing to the stereo angle 𝛼 of the skewed layers, the position of this intersection along the wire is directly correlated with the longitudinal position of the track. A collection of (mostly) Python3 scripts to facilitate the use of the LuminosityFit software.

Note that the whole workflow is far from trivial, and there are many details that are not mentioned in this Readme.

The LuminosityFit software requires a reconstructed elastic scattering events from the Panda Luminosity Detector (LMD).

As long as the [PANDA experiment](https://panda.gsi.de/) is not running these events have to be simulated using the PandaRoot framework.

Simulations and reconstruction can be easily performed using the python scripts `doSimulationReconstruction.py` or `doReconstruction.py`. Use the `--help` flag to get more detailed information on how to use these scripts. These scripts create so call configuration files `sim_params.config` and `reco_params.config`, that contain all of the information to perform a simulation or reconstruction (as you specified them).

The are useful for bookkeeping and can also be used to redo the simulation or reconstruction using the scripts `runSimulationReconstruction.py` and `runReconstruction.py`.

Note that the simulation step also can create an `elastic_cross_section.txt` file when the dpm mode is selected. It contains the cross section of the elastic scattering process, corresponding to the generated events. From this the reference luminosity can be calculated, which is useful for calculating the accuracy of the luminosity determination procedure.

Once you have an unfiltered (do **NOT** use any cut flags in the reconstruction, such as `--use_xy_cut` or `--use_m_cut`) dataset of reconstructed elastic scattering events, the luminosity determination can be started.

Use `determineLuminosity.py`, which is quite complicated and *fragile*, and only runs on the Himster2 cluster in Mainz. The reason for this is that the whole luminosity determination process is very difficult. The excellent accuracy in the below percent level can only be reached with big efforts. Currently the efficiency and resolution corrections are performed via additional simulations and reconstruction.

The overall steps in the luminosity determination process are:

1. create interaction point (IP) distribution from the unfiltered reconstructed elastic scattering tracks
2. determine the means (X,Y,Z) of the IP distribution
3. filter the elastic scattering dataset 
   **AND** independently do a simulation and reconstruction using the determined IP info and a box generator
4. create a 2D angular track distribution of the filtered elastic scattering dataset 
   **AND** independently create an efficiency and a resolution object from the box generated dataset
5. perform the actual luminosity fit using the 2D angular track distribution and the efficiency and resolution objects

These step exclude a possible alignment process which should run before all of this.

Figure 20 : Simulation model of the luminosity detector.
By looking at the complete flow-chart of the software package (figure 21 ) one can see the workflow of the LMD software. The LMD fit procedure, which determines the luminosity from the angular antiproton distribution, requires three essential inputs: the reconstructed tracks arising from the actual measured detector hits, the detector acceptance and the detector resolution. In order to obtain this information several data processing steps are required, that can be categorized into three stages.
alignment stage : At first in the so called alignment stage the misalignment of each individual sensor has to be detected with respect to its reference position in the ¯ PANDA coordinate system. The alignment itself consists of three parts, the alignment of the sensors on a module, the alignment of modules within a corridor and the alignment of the corridors to the global ¯ PANDA reference frame [ 102 ]. Usually the alignment procedure only has to be performed once after the detector has been physically undergone changes, i.e initial setup or retraction/insertion of the detector halves. While the first two alignment parts are crucial for the correct reconstruction of particle track parameters, the third part is elementary for correct determination of the displacement of the IP and the accelerator beam tilt.
acceptance and resolution parameterizations : As a second step the detector acceptance and detector resolution parameterization are computed by using a MC data sample and by using the IP position information from the first stage.
data reconstruction The third stage consists of the track reconstruction from the measured data, which has to be corrected for the misalignment of the sensors.
Note that the second and third step are only dependent on step 1 , hence they are not time-ordered with respect to each other. All three stages share the same track recon- struction software. Figure 22 provides a zoom-in into stage 3 of figure 21 . The complete reconstruction chain is separated into 6 steps, each performing a specific task going from the raw pixel data to the fully reconstructed track at the IP [ 98 ].

For many studies we need lots of simulation data from different boundary conditions (rest gas, misalignment and so on), automated reconstruction and luminosity fits. For these, we've included two scripts that automate almost everything in the `python` directory.

./runSimulationReconstruction.py -e expConfig/PANDA/1.5.config

This script is done pretty fast, but it does submit a lot of jobs. Check on these with `squeue -u YOUR_USERNAME`. Once all are done, run:

```
./determineLuminosity.py -e expConfig/PANDA/1.5.config
```

This may take a few hours.

4. Local Reconstruction:
The digitized data is subject of a local reconstruction procedure which associates
DigiHits to information with a physical meaning, like a 3D space point, a total
energy loss or a Cherenkov angle. For tracking sub-systems during this step track
reconstruction is done, which usually includes track search and track ﬁt.
5. Global Reconstruction:
At this stage, locally reconstructed information is sorted to produce valuable input
for further analysis. This sorting procedure can include assignment between re-
constructed data from diﬀerent subsystems as well as merge of local information
to improve reconstructed parameters (i.g two parts of one charged particle track
in neighboring subsystems). Particle identiﬁcation at Panda is performed globally,
taking into account information from all sub-detectors.
6. Physics Analysis:
The analysis tools have to deal with a collection of information based on four-
momenta, positions and the identity of the reconstructed particles in a uniﬁed
way.
Particle combination, selection mechanisms and manipulation tools (like
boosting between lab and center of mass frame) are provided. Furthermore, a set
of ﬁtters is available to ﬁt the four momenta and positions of particles (e.g. from
a decay) under diﬀerent types of constraints.
For the luminosity measurement, only information from the luminosity detector is
essential. This means only locally reconstructed information is used and steps 5 and 6
are not needed. Fig. 4.1 shows the reconstruction chain in the LMD step by step, starting
with hit reconstruction up to back propagation of tracks to the interaction point. In the

of the ¯pp elastic scattering in the PANDA energy range by the future KOALA experiment.
As a detector, the LMD is a small tracking system, which will be inserted 11m down-
stream from the IP. It is designed to measure the forward scattered antiprotons with
angles between 3 and 8mrad in polar angle and the full azimuth angle. The LMD con-
sists of 4 planes, each plane contains 10 modules with pixel sensors (HV-MAPS), sen-
sitive to the position of the track. For the determination of the luminosity, the cross
section in dependence on the scattering angle has to be extracted from the data. The
data reconstruction includes several crucial steps: ﬁnding and ﬁtting of the tracks of
the elastically scattered antiprotons and backtracking them to the interaction point in
order to get rid of the inﬂuence of the magnetic ﬁeld, which the particles pass before
reaching the LMD.
Fig. 8.1 demonstrates how the luminosity will be extracted from raw data1. The
data treatment starts with the determination of alignment parameters and variables
needed to tune the simulation (e.g exact position of the IP). As a second step, the two-
dimensional functions for the acceptance and the detector resolution are extracted from
the Monte Carlo simulation with a realistic model of the detector. Then the data for the
luminosity ﬁt are reconstructed taking the misalignment of the detector components
into account and cleaned from background contributions.
Although the material budget of the LMD is very low, the remaining material af-
fects the resolution of low momentum tracks by multiple scattering. To overcome this
problem, the Cellular Automaton (CA) algorithm was implemented in addition to the
more simple Track Following (TF) algorithm for the track search. It was shown that CA
deals better with high multiplicity events at low energies. For the Track Fit, multiple
scattering is taken into account by the "breaking-lines" approach. Another feature
of the reconstruction chain is the back propagation of the tracks to the IP. The back
propagation of the track parameters works ﬁne, however it was shown that the extrap-
olation of the co-variance matrix is not accurate enough and should be studied more
carefully. The track reconstruction chain was checked in diﬀerent simulation tests and
extensively used in diﬀerent steps needed for the accurate luminosity determination.
In order to achieve the best resolution for the scattering angle measurement, even
a misalignment of 50 µm between modules has to be avoided. This potential problem
was attacked with a software alignment method based on reconstructed tracks. The
Millipede algorithm is a widely used solution for this task, because it allows the deter-
mination of all alignment parameters in a simultaneous linear least squares ﬁt with an
arbitrary number of tracks. Due to the fact that the LMD prototype does not exist yet
and the real misalignment scale is not known, extensive tests were made to prove that
the Millipede algorithm is applicable for the LMD.
Another open question is how many tracks of background reactions, mainly of in-
elastic antiproton proton reactions, will reach the LMD. Diﬀerent background sources

The LuminosityFit software requires a reconstructed elastic scattering events from the Panda Luminosity Detector (LMD).

As long as the [PANDA experiment](https://panda.gsi.de/) is not running these events have to be simulated using the PandaRoot framework.

Simulations and reconstruction can be easily performed using the python scripts `doSimulationReconstruction.py` or `doReconstruction.py`. Use the `--help` flag to get more detailed information on how to use these scripts. These scripts create so call configuration files `sim_params.config` and `reco_params.config`, that contain all of the information to perform a simulation or reconstruction (as you specified them).

The are useful for bookkeeping and can also be used to redo the simulation or reconstruction using the scripts `runSimulationReconstruction.py` and `runReconstruction.py`.

Note that the simulation step also can create an `elastic_cross_section.txt` file when the dpm mode is selected. It contains the cross section of the elastic scattering process, corresponding to the generated events. From this the reference luminosity can be calculated, which is useful for calculating the accuracy of the luminosity determination procedure.

Once you have an unfiltered (do **NOT** use any cut flags in the reconstruction, such as `--use_xy_cut` or `--use_m_cut`) dataset of reconstructed elastic scattering events, the luminosity determination can be started.

Use `determineLuminosity.py`, which is quite complicated and *fragile*, and only runs on the Himster2 cluster in Mainz. The reason for this is that the whole luminosity determination process is very difficult. The excellent accuracy in the below percent level can only be reached with big efforts. Currently the efficiency and resolution corrections are performed via additional simulations and reconstruction.

The overall steps in the luminosity determination process are:

1. create interaction point (IP) distribution from the unfiltered reconstructed elastic scattering tracks
2. determine the means (X,Y,Z) of the IP distribution
3. filter the elastic scattering dataset 
   **AND** independently do a simulation and reconstruction using the determined IP info and a box generator
4. create a 2D angular track distribution of the filtered elastic scattering dataset 
   **AND** independently create an efficiency and a resolution object from the box generated dataset
5. perform the actual luminosity fit using the 2D angular track distribution and the efficiency and resolution objects

These step exclude a possible alignment process which should run before all of this.

import subprocess

import os

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(

)

    "num_events",

)

    "--low_index",

To overcome the severe limitations of simple analytical parameterizations, the Dual Parton Model (DPM) is employed as a robust phenomenological framework to describe high-energy ¯ 𝑝𝑝 elastic scattering [124, 125]. For the specific purpose of luminosity determination at PANDA, the primary practical advantage of the DPM lies in its ability to accurately model the hadronic amplitude across a wide range of momentum transfers ( | 𝑡 | ) without relying on unstable free parameters. Simple exponential parameterizations of the hadronic amplitude (e.g., 𝑒 -𝑏 | 𝑡 | ) via Eq. 3.6 are valid only at small momentum transfers [126, 127]. They completely fail to describe the complex diffractive structures, such as pronounced dips and secondary maxima, that inherently appear at larger | 𝑡 | values in ¯ 𝑝𝑝 scattering. Furthermore, attempting to extract the luminosity by treating fundamental variables like 𝜎 𝑡𝑜𝑡 , 𝑏 , and 𝜌 as independent free parameters for every single energy scan point can easily lead to unphysical mathematical fluctuations in the fit results. To overcome these experimental and phenomenological limitations, a more complicated DPM-based model is employed [128]:

To accurately simulate the physical processes, the detector geometry is first meticulously modeled based on the ROOT framework, organized as a hierarchical nesting of volumes called assemblies. The basic physical volumes are translated and rotated to form these higher-level assemblies. Because the tree of assemblies is accessed via a directory of their names, identifying specific sensors requires a full structural path. To streamline this process during data processing, the PndGeoHandling class is utilized to dynamically map the sensitive physical volumes to unique integer identifiers known as sensor IDs. Furthermore, to optimize computational performance, only interactions within predefined active volumes (e.g., designated by names like 'PixelActive') are evaluated and stored.
The data processing pipeline, illustrated in detail in Figure 2.18, begins with MonteCarlo Transport and Digitization . Primary particles generated by event generators are propagated through the detector geometry and magnetic field via the Virtual Monte Carlo (VMC) interface (utilizing engines like GEANT3 or GEANT4). Whenever a simulated particle traverses an active silicon volume managed by PndSdsDetector , a Monte-Carlo point ( SdsMCPoint ) is instantiated. This point records crucial exact physical quantities, including the entry and exit coordinates, momentum, energy loss within the volume, and the precise time of flight.
Subsequently, the SdsHitProducer executes the digitization process. Digitization simulates the specific electronic response of the detector, converting the continuous energy loss of the SdsMCPoint into discrete digital signals ( SdsDigi , specialized as PndSdsDigiPixel or PndSdsDigiStrip ). Chapter9 Summary of the Luminosity
Determination
The capability of the PANDA detector, specifically the upgraded Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) utilizing HVMAPS technology has been established, to perform a precise, data-driven measurement of the Restgas density profile over the full range of 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m. The superior vertexing resolution and reduced material budget of the sensors are critical factors that enable the effective determination of the Restgas distribution even for interactions significantly displaced from the nominal IP.
Through the implementation of a profile-dependent efficiency correction and a robust iterative workflow, the systematic distortions caused by resolution smearing and initial model inaccuracies are rigorously suppressed. This method acts as a contracting map, converging to the true physical distribution and ensuring that the final result is independent of the initial simulation input provided by the Target Group. To quantify the stability of this approach, an iterative procedure was initialized with an extreme starting condition: a 40% overestimation of the Restgas distribution. As summarized in Table 9.1, the iterative procedure converges rapidly. Within merely three steps, the global deviation drops from 12 . 27% to 1 . 30%, and the deviation in the central region vanishes to -0 . 22%. Consequently, the precise density profile can be derived directly from the experimental data across the entire relevant domain, providing the reliable input essential for the absolute luminosity determination.
Finally, the determined Restgas profile was integrated back into the LuminosityFit framework to validate the complete analysis chain. The luminosity determination was performed at a beam momentum of 𝑝 𝑏𝑒𝑎𝑚 = 4 . 06 GeV /𝑐 , applying a cut within the analysis window ( | 𝑥 | , | 𝑦 | < 1 cm and | 𝑧 | < 5 cm). The relative deviation of the determined luminosity (Δ ℒ / ℒ ) is (0 . 05 ± 0 . 07)% with the reconstructed target profile with Restgas background. As presented in Table 9.2, this result is consistent with the ideal case where the target is treated as point-like and the efficiency correction is based on a point-like model, which yields a deviation of -0 . 036 ± 0 . 07% and also with the case where the target profile with Restgas background is well-known and totally the same as real data, which yields a deviation of 0 . 02 ± 0 . 08%. This results demonstrate that the synergy of high-precision tracking and advanced fitting algorithms transforms the Restgas background from a limiting systematic background into a precisely monitored observable, enabling a robust and accurate luminosity determination for the PANDA experiment.
