raw.text:
To balance speed and performance, a multi-layered selection strategy is adopted. Rather than treating the STT as a uniform cloud of hits, the algorithm analyzes the hit distribution row by row. To maximize the geometric lever arm for curvature determination, the hits are categorized into inner, mid, and outer rows based on their radial position. The algorithm prioritizes triplets formed by selecting one hit from each of these distinct regions (Inner → Mid → Outer). This long-baseline selection ensures that the triplet spans the maximum available track length, resulting in a stable and precise circle fit. Within this radial framework, a further reduction of candidates is achieved using a strategy inspired by Cellular Automata. The detector is segmented into angular sectors in 𝜑 , and spatially adjacent STT hits that form a continuous chain are grouped into segments. The search for triplet partners is then restricted to hits that are both topologically connected and 𝜑 -compatible. Specifically, the second and third hits must be reachable via the neighbor map, ensuring that the combination follows the particle's path through the straw tubes. In addition, the hits are required to lie within a compatible angular range in 𝜑 , thereby rejecting combinations that would imply unphysical 'zig-zag' trajectories.
Reconstruction Strategy
121
This two-tiered approach-first defining the radial strategy (Inner/Mid/Outer) to ensure quality, then using neighbor connectivity to ensure speed-allows the Apollonius tracker finder to reconstruct displaced tracks with high efficiency while keeping the computing time manageable.
Solving the Apollonius Problem Once a valid triplet is formed by selecting one hit from each of the distinct radial groups (Inner, Mid, and Outer rows), it serves as a geometric seed. The algorithm then proceeds to determine the full track parameters through a 'Hypothesis and Test' approach.
Step 1: Calculation of Candidate Trajectories. The three selected drift circles define a classical Problem of Apollonius. From a mathematical standpoint, up to eight distinct circles can be constructed that are simultaneously tangent to three given circles, corresponding to the different combinations of internal and external tangency. The algorithm analytically computes the parameters ( 𝑥 𝑐 , 𝑦 𝑐 , 𝑅 ) for all eight solutions. Each of these solutions represents a track hypothesis, reflecting the possible particle trajectories arising from the left-right ambiguities of the drift tube measurements.
Step 2: Hit Assignment (Track Growing). To identify which of these hypotheses corresponds to a physical particle, the algorithm validates each candidate against the full set of available STT hits. For every Apollonius circle, a search is performed over the axial hits, and a hit is assigned to the candidate if its measured drift distance is consistent with the circle trajectory within a predefined tolerance. Through this procedure, the purely mathematical solutions are transformed into populated track candidates.
Step 3: Selection of the Proper Circle. The final step is the selection of the proper physical trajectory among the populated candidates. This choice is based on a composite quality metric that combines topological, statistical, and geometric considerations. First, the algorithm checks the continuity of the assigned hits, requiring that they form a topologically connected and nearly gap-free chain along the straw tubes; candidates that produce fragmented or discontinuous segments are rejected. Among the remaining solutions, preference is given to the candidate that associates the largest number of hits, as a trajectory supported by more measurements is statistically more robust than one constrained only by the initial triplet.

Precise Measurement of the Restgas Distribution
This section details the modifications implemented in the PandaRoot framework to achieve precise track reconstruction and particle identification for events originating away from the nominal IP.
The analysis presented in this work is based on the PandaRoot framework, version oct19 . This specific release was selected to ensure the stability of the tracking algorithms. Newer iterations of the framework were found to exhibit regressions in the primary track reconstruction quality even for standard events at the origin, necessitating the use of the robust oct19 release as the baseline for this study.
Tracking for Displaced Vertices: The Apollonius Algorithm
The first stage of track reconstruction is the track finding. The standard tracking algorithms in PANDA (e.g., the Barrel Track Finder) generally optimize performance by imposing a constraint that tracks must originate from the primary vertex region ( 𝑥 ≈ 𝑦 ≈ 0). While effective for the nominal IP, this assumption leads to inefficiencies and systematic biases when reconstructing tracks from displaced vertices, such as those arising from interactions with Restgas particles or shifted beam-target collisions.
In the case of interactions with Restgas particles, the reaction vertices are distributed along the beam axis ( 𝑧 ) and can exhibit transverse offsets. To recover these displaced tracks, which topologically resemble secondary decay products, a track finder developed for secondary vertices called Apollonius Triplet Track Finder was integrated into the reconstruction chain [147, 148].
The reconstruction of displaced tracks is implemented as a two-stage process within the PandaRoot framework. The first stage performs pattern recognition in the 𝑥𝑦 -plane using the axial STT layers. The second stage recovers the longitudinal ( 𝑧 ) information using the skewed STT layers.
The algorithm is mathematically grounded in the classical Problem of Apollonius (circa 200 BC), which seeks to construct a circle that is tangent to three given circles. Unlike global Hough transforms, this algorithm constructs tracks locally from triplets of hits. The implementation of the algorithm within the PandaRoot framework addresses two main computational challenges: the combinatorial selection of hits and the ambiguity of the geometric solution.
Triplet Selection Strategy The first step of the algorithm, selecting three STT hits ( ℎ 1 , ℎ 2 , ℎ 3 ) to form a triplet, is critical. A brute-force combination of all available hits would result in an unmanageable combinatorial explosion. Conversely, if the selection criteria are too tight, valid tracks might be discarded, leading to a drop in efficiency.

For candidates with comparable hit counts, the geometric fit quality is evaluated by computing the quadratic distance of the assigned hits to the candidate circle,
where 𝑑 𝑖 denotes the distance from the center of the 𝑖 -th hit to the track center and 𝑅 is the track radius. The solution that minimizes this quantity, corresponding to the best overall geometric consistency, is selected as the final track seed. This robust selection procedure ensures that the algorithm does not merely identify a mathematical circle passing through three points, but reconstructs a physically meaningful trajectory that is supported by the maximum amount of detector information.
Longitudinal Reconstruction (Skewed Straw Pz Finder)
The two-dimensional circles obtained from the Apollonius step fully define the track curvature in the 𝑥𝑦 -plane, but they do not provide any information on the longitudinal coordinate 𝑧 . The reconstruction of the third dimension is therefore performed in a subsequent step by the Pz Finder, which exploits the specific geometry of the skewed STT layers that are tilted by ± 2 . 9 ∘ with respect to the beam axis.
Starting from the two-dimensional track candidates, the algorithm searches for hits in the skewed straw layers that are geometrically compatible with the extrapolated 2D circle. Once such hits are identified, the intersection between the cylindrical surface defined by the 2D track and the corresponding skewed straw wire which is modeled as a straight line in three-dimensional space is calculated. Owing to the stereo angle 𝛼 of the skewed layers, the position of this intersection along the wire is directly correlated with the longitudinal position of the track. The 𝑧 -coordinate of each intersection point is obtained according to
where 𝜑 int denotes the azimuthal angle of the intersection and 𝑅 is the track radius, 𝛼 is the aforementioned stereo angle defining the wire inclination, and 𝑧 0 represents the longitudinal offset of the track (i.e., its 𝑧 -coordinate at the reference azimuth 𝜑 = 0).
By accumulating multiple measurements from different skewed layers, the algorithm performs a linear regression in the 𝑠 -𝑧 plane, with 𝑠 = 𝑅𝜑 representing the arc length along the track. The slope of this fit determines the dip angle 𝜆 and, consequently, the longitudinal momentum component 𝑝 𝑧 , while the intercept yields the 𝑧 -position of the track origin. By decoupling the pattern recognition in the transverse plane from the longitudinal reconstruction, this method enables the efficient reconstruction of tracks with arbitrary production points, making it particularly well suited for recovering Restgas events distributed along the beam axis.

Reconstruction Strategy
123
Integration with MVD and GEM (Global Tracking)
The output of the combined Apollonius and Pz Finder stages is a track seed based solely on STT information. While this seed is highly effective for identifying displaced tracks, it does not yet provide the precision required for accurate vertex reconstruction. The full integration of information from all tracking sub-detectors is therefore performed in the final Kalman filtering stage.
The Apollonius algorithm supplies an initial track candidate derived from STT isochrones, which defines a preliminary trajectory but does not include the highprecision measurements from the silicon-based detectors. These track candidates are subsequently processed by the KalmanFit using the GenFit framework, which applies a statistically rigorous Kalman filter to combine measurements from different detector systems. During this procedure, the STT-based helix is extrapolated inward toward the MVD volume, where compatible pixel or strip hits are searched for and, if found, incorporated into the track. This inward propagation significantly improves the resolution of the impact parameters 𝑑 0 and 𝑧 0 and is crucial for precisely locating the interaction vertex. In parallel, the track is extrapolated outward to the GEM stations, where additional measurements refine the momentum determination, particularly for forward-going particles, leading to an improved relative momentum resolution 𝑑𝑝/𝑝 .
As a result, the final reconstructed tracks coherently combine information from all tracking subsystems-MVD, STT, and GEM-leveraging the large acceptance and pattern recognition capability of the STT together with the superior spatial resolution of the MVD and GEM to achieve precise vertex and momentum reconstruction.
PID Step
The accurate determination of particle kinematics relies not only on precise track fitting but also on the correct association of reconstructed tracks with their physical interaction vertex during the PID step. Track candidates produced by the track finder are represented as infinite helices extending throughout the detector volume. Consequently, a crucial task of the PID step is the determination of the true physical origin of these trajectories, in order to effectively anchor and terminate them at their source. Without a well-defined starting point, essential kinematic quantities-most notably the momentum vector and the path length required for energy-loss corrections-cannot be uniquely or reliably determined.
This issue becomes particularly severe in the presence of Restgas background, where interactions occur at arbitrary locations along and within the beam pipe rather than being confined to the nominal target region. Under these conditions, the IP determination approach in the PID step must be reconsidered.
Limitations of the Standard Approach: In the standard PandaRoot workflow, a strong geometric constraint is imposed by assuming that particle trajectories originate from the beam axis near the nominal interaction point. As a result, tracks identified by the finder are processed by a Kalman Filter and typically propagated forward by ≈ 2 cm, then Kalman-fitted tracks are propagated to the point of closest approach to the 𝑧 -axis (POCA-to-line), which is then used to define the reference momentum vector and path length for the PID step.

While this approximation is well justified for interactions localized within the target region, it leads to significant systematic biases when applied to interactions with Restgas particles. Owing to the beam complication and the extended longitudinal density profile of the Restgas background, such interactions are distributed stochastically along the vacuum pipe and may exhibit substantial displacements in both transverse ( 𝑥, 𝑦 ) and longitudinal ( 𝑧 ) directions. Forcing a helical trajectory to reference the beam axis when its true origin is displaced by several centimeters can result in severe reconstruction distortions. In particular, transverse offsets may cause the geometric solver to fail or produce ambiguous solutions, while longitudinal displacements lead to an incorrect estimation of the particle's flight path through the detector material. This path-length miscalculation directly affects the energyloss ( 𝑑𝐸/𝑑𝑥 ) correction and introduces a systematic bias in the reconstructed polar angle 𝜃 , as the momentum vector is effectively evaluated at an unphysical reference plane.
Modified POCA-First Approach: To address these topological limitations, a modified reconstruction scheme, referred to as the POCA-First Approach , was developed. Starting from the global track candidates seeded by the Apollonius finder and produced by the Kalman filter, the algorithm analytically computes the threedimensional point of closest approach (POCA) of all the tracks of the elastically scattered ¯ 𝑝𝑝 events. The resulting coordinate, ⃗ 𝑣 POCA , provides an estimator of the true interaction vertex and serves as the physical anchor point for subsequent kinematic reconstruction.
Once the geometric vertex ⃗ 𝑣 POCA is established, the Kalman-fitted tracks perform a targeted back-propagation. The track parameters are propagated from the outer detectors back specifically to the point of closest approach, to the 3D coordinate ⃗ 𝑣 POCA (POCA-to-point), rather than to the 𝑧 -axis. This POCA-to-point back-propagation effectively reconstructs the IP for displaced vertices, ensuring that the track parameters are evaluated at the actual interaction location. It is at this location that the momentum vector is evaluated, and the path length is determined for the energy loss calculation. This ensures that the PID algorithms receive kinematic inputs that correctly reflect the particle's history through the detector material and magnetic field up to the actual point of interaction.
By anchoring the track parameters to the reconstructed interaction vertex rather than an arbitrary axis, this approach effectively eliminates the systematic biases introduced by displaced vertices, thereby enabling accurate IP and momentum reconstruction and particle identification for events from beam-Restgas interactions. The validity of using this calculated geometric estimator was rigorously verified through simulation studies.

raw.text: the target spectrometer For the determination of momenta of charged particles one requires tracking detectors and a magnetic field. The barrel part has a solenoid magnet with a magnetic field strength of 2 T around the IP and several tracking detectors. The most inner detector surrounding the IP is the micro vertex detector [ 85 ]. It is a combination of semiconductor strip sensors and pixel sensors in the regions of high track multiplicities delivering the high vertex resolution of below 100 µ m . Both the primary interaction vertex and secondary vertices of short lived particles and delayed decays rely on information of the micro vertex detector (MVD). Furthermore it improves the momentum resolution and PID. Just surrounding the MVD is the central tracker, the straw tube tracker (STT) [ 86 ] consisting of a total of 4636 straws. A straw is a 10 mm thick aluminised mylar tube, which is operated with an ArCO 2 gas mixture at an overpressure of 1 bar , making it self-supporting. Each straw tube contains a single anode wire in the centre, collection the generated charge clouds. They are arranged in planar layers around the beam pipe at radial distances 15 cm -41 . 8 cm and an overall length of 150 cm . The detector delivers position resolutions of less than 150 µ m with a material budget of 1 . 2 % of one radiation length at a momentum range from about a few 100 MeV/c up to 8 GeV/c . In addition energy loss (dE/dx) for the particle trajectories can be calculated, which is needed in particular to separate protons, kaons and pions in the momentum region below 1 GeV/c . Particles emitted at angles below 20 ° are not covered by the STT and will be tracked by three planar gas electron multiplier (GEM) stations placed approximately 1 . 1 m , 1 . 4 m and 1 . 9 m downstream of the target. The GEMs are able to sustain the high particle rates in the forward direction due to the relativistic boost of the fixed target setup and enable unambiguous tracking with a position resolution below 100 µ m .

To balance speed and performance, a multi-layered selection strategy is adopted. Rather than treating the STT as a uniform cloud of hits, the algorithm analyzes the hit distribution row by row. To maximize the geometric lever arm for curvature determination, the hits are categorized into inner, mid, and outer rows based on their radial position. The algorithm prioritizes triplets formed by selecting one hit from each of these distinct regions (Inner → Mid → Outer). This long-baseline selection ensures that the triplet spans the maximum available track length, resulting in a stable and precise circle fit. Within this radial framework, a further reduction of candidates is achieved using a strategy inspired by Cellular Automata. The detector is segmented into angular sectors in 𝜑 , and spatially adjacent STT hits that form a continuous chain are grouped into segments. The search for triplet partners is then restricted to hits that are both topologically connected and 𝜑 -compatible. Specifically, the second and third hits must be reachable via the neighbor map, ensuring that the combination follows the particle's path through the straw tubes. In addition, the hits are required to lie within a compatible angular range in 𝜑 , thereby rejecting combinations that would imply unphysical 'zig-zag' trajectories.

This two-tiered approach-first defining the radial strategy (Inner/Mid/Outer) to ensure quality, then using neighbor connectivity to ensure speed-allows the Apollonius tracker finder to reconstruct displaced tracks with high efficiency while keeping the computing time manageable.
Solving the Apollonius Problem Once a valid triplet is formed by selecting one hit from each of the distinct radial groups (Inner, Mid, and Outer rows), it serves as a geometric seed. The algorithm then proceeds to determine the full track parameters through a 'Hypothesis and Test' approach.
Step 1: Calculation of Candidate Trajectories. The three selected drift circles define a classical Problem of Apollonius. From a mathematical standpoint, up to eight distinct circles can be constructed that are simultaneously tangent to three given circles, corresponding to the different combinations of internal and external tangency. The algorithm analytically computes the parameters ( 𝑥 𝑐 , 𝑦 𝑐 , 𝑅 ) for all eight solutions. Each of these solutions represents a track hypothesis, reflecting the possible particle trajectories arising from the left-right ambiguities of the drift tube measurements.
Step 2: Hit Assignment (Track Growing). To identify which of these hypotheses corresponds to a physical particle, the algorithm validates each candidate against the full set of available STT hits. For every Apollonius circle, a search is performed over the axial hits, and a hit is assigned to the candidate if its measured drift distance is consistent with the circle trajectory within a predefined tolerance. Through this procedure, the purely mathematical solutions are transformed into populated track candidates.
Step 3: Selection of the Proper Circle. The final step is the selection of the proper physical trajectory among the populated candidates. This choice is based on a composite quality metric that combines topological, statistical, and geometric considerations. First, the algorithm checks the continuity of the assigned hits, requiring that they form a topologically connected and nearly gap-free chain along the straw tubes; candidates that produce fragmented or discontinuous segments are rejected. Among the remaining solutions, preference is given to the candidate that associates the largest number of hits, as a trajectory supported by more measurements is statistically more robust than one constrained only by the initial triplet.

This section details the modifications implemented in the PandaRoot framework to achieve precise track reconstruction and particle identification for events originating away from the nominal IP.
The analysis presented in this work is based on the PandaRoot framework, version oct19 . This specific release was selected to ensure the stability of the tracking algorithms. Newer iterations of the framework were found to exhibit regressions in the primary track reconstruction quality even for standard events at the origin, necessitating the use of the robust oct19 release as the baseline for this study.
Tracking for Displaced Vertices: The Apollonius Algorithm
The first stage of track reconstruction is the track finding. The standard tracking algorithms in PANDA (e.g., the Barrel Track Finder) generally optimize performance by imposing a constraint that tracks must originate from the primary vertex region ( 𝑥 ≈ 𝑦 ≈ 0). While effective for the nominal IP, this assumption leads to inefficiencies and systematic biases when reconstructing tracks from displaced vertices, such as those arising from interactions with Restgas particles or shifted beam-target collisions.
In the case of interactions with Restgas particles, the reaction vertices are distributed along the beam axis ( 𝑧 ) and can exhibit transverse offsets. To recover these displaced tracks, which topologically resemble secondary decay products, a track finder developed for secondary vertices called Apollonius Triplet Track Finder was integrated into the reconstruction chain [147, 148].
The reconstruction of displaced tracks is implemented as a two-stage process within the PandaRoot framework. The first stage performs pattern recognition in the 𝑥𝑦 -plane using the axial STT layers. The second stage recovers the longitudinal ( 𝑧 ) information using the skewed STT layers.
The algorithm is mathematically grounded in the classical Problem of Apollonius (circa 200 BC), which seeks to construct a circle that is tangent to three given circles. Unlike global Hough transforms, this algorithm constructs tracks locally from triplets of hits. The implementation of the algorithm within the PandaRoot framework addresses two main computational challenges: the combinatorial selection of hits and the ambiguity of the geometric solution.
Triplet Selection Strategy The first step of the algorithm, selecting three STT hits ( ℎ 1 , ℎ 2 , ℎ 3 ) to form a triplet, is critical. A brute-force combination of all available hits would result in an unmanageable combinatorial explosion. Conversely, if the selection criteria are too tight, valid tracks might be discarded, leading to a drop in efficiency.

### 3.2 Displaced-track reconstruction

Standard primary-track finders often assume that tracks originate close to the nominal beam axis. This is inappropriate for Restgas interactions distributed over a long region.

The dedicated reconstruction chain is configured in:

- `macro/target/reco_complete.C`

Its relevant stages are:

1. `PndTrkTracking2` performs the standard reconstruction.
2. `PndUnassignedHitsTask` collects hits not assigned by the standard track finder.
3. `PndApolloniusTripletTrackFinderTask` reconstructs displaced trajectories using STT drift-circle triplets and MVD/GEM information.
4. `PndSttSkewStrawPzFinderTask` recovers the longitudinal track component from skewed STT layers.
5. `PndRecoKalmanTask2` fits the resulting tracks with `SetPropagateToIP(kFALSE)`.

This robust selection procedure ensures that the algorithm does not merely identify a mathematical circle passing through three points, but reconstructs a physically meaningful trajectory that is supported by the maximum amount of detector information.
Longitudinal Reconstruction (Skewed Straw Pz Finder)
The two-dimensional circles obtained from the Apollonius step fully define the track curvature in the 𝑥𝑦 -plane, but they do not provide any information on the longitudinal coordinate 𝑧 . The reconstruction of the third dimension is therefore performed in a subsequent step by the Pz Finder, which exploits the specific geometry of the skewed STT layers that are tilted by ± 2 . 9 ∘ with respect to the beam axis.
Starting from the two-dimensional track candidates, the algorithm searches for hits in the skewed straw layers that are geometrically compatible with the extrapolated 2D circle. Once such hits are identified, the intersection between the cylindrical surface defined by the 2D track and the corresponding skewed straw wire which is modeled as a straight line in three-dimensional space is calculated. Owing to the stereo angle 𝛼 of the skewed layers, the position of this intersection along the wire is directly correlated with the longitudinal position of the track. The 𝑧 -coordinate of each intersection point is obtained according to
where 𝜑 int denotes the azimuthal angle of the intersection and 𝑅 is the track radius, 𝛼 is the aforementioned stereo angle defining the wire inclination, and 𝑧 0 represents the longitudinal offset of the track (i.e., its 𝑧 -coordinate at the reference azimuth 𝜑 = 0).
By accumulating multiple measurements from different skewed layers, the algorithm performs a linear regression in the 𝑠 -𝑧 plane, with 𝑠 = 𝑅𝜑 representing the arc length along the track. The slope of this fit determines the dip angle 𝜆 and, consequently, the longitudinal momentum component 𝑝 𝑧 , while the intercept yields the 𝑧 -position of the track origin. By decoupling the pattern recognition in the transverse plane from the longitudinal reconstruction, this method enables the efficient reconstruction of tracks with arbitrary production points, making it particularly well suited for recovering Restgas events distributed along the beam axis.

Limitations of the Standard Approach: In the standard PandaRoot workflow, a strong geometric constraint is imposed by assuming that particle trajectories originate from the beam axis near the nominal interaction point. As a result, tracks identified by the finder are processed by a Kalman Filter and typically propagated forward by ≈ 2 cm, then Kalman-fitted tracks are propagated to the point of closest approach to the 𝑧 -axis (POCA-to-line), which is then used to define the reference momentum vector and path length for the PID step.
124
Precise Measurement of the Restgas Distribution
While this approximation is well justified for interactions localized within the target region, it leads to significant systematic biases when applied to interactions with Restgas particles. Owing to the beam complication and the extended longitudinal density profile of the Restgas background, such interactions are distributed stochastically along the vacuum pipe and may exhibit substantial displacements in both transverse ( 𝑥, 𝑦 ) and longitudinal ( 𝑧 ) directions. Forcing a helical trajectory to reference the beam axis when its true origin is displaced by several centimeters can result in severe reconstruction distortions. In particular, transverse offsets may cause the geometric solver to fail or produce ambiguous solutions, while longitudinal displacements lead to an incorrect estimation of the particle's flight path through the detector material. This path-length miscalculation directly affects the energyloss ( 𝑑𝐸/𝑑𝑥 ) correction and introduces a systematic bias in the reconstructed polar angle 𝜃 , as the momentum vector is effectively evaluated at an unphysical reference plane.
Modified POCA-First Approach: To address these topological limitations, a modified reconstruction scheme, referred to as the POCA-First Approach , was developed. Starting from the global track candidates seeded by the Apollonius finder and produced by the Kalman filter, the algorithm analytically computes the threedimensional point of closest approach (POCA) of all the tracks of the elastically scattered ¯ 𝑝𝑝 events. The resulting coordinate, ⃗ 𝑣 POCA , provides an estimator of the true interaction vertex and serves as the physical anchor point for subsequent kinematic reconstruction.
Once the geometric vertex ⃗ 𝑣 POCA is established, the Kalman-fitted tracks perform a targeted back-propagation. The track parameters are propagated from the outer detectors back specifically to the point of closest approach, to the 3D coordinate ⃗ 𝑣 POCA (POCA-to-point), rather than to the 𝑧 -axis. This POCA-to-point back-propagation effectively reconstructs the IP for displaced vertices, ensuring that the track parameters are evaluated at the actual interaction location. It is at this location that the momentum vector is evaluated, and the path length is determined for the energy loss calculation. This ensures that the PID algorithms receive kinematic inputs that correctly reflect the particle's history through the detector material and magnetic field up to the actual point of interaction.
By anchoring the track parameters to the reconstructed interaction vertex rather than an arbitrary axis, this approach effectively eliminates the systematic biases introduced by displaced vertices, thereby enabling accurate IP and momentum reconstruction and particle identification for events from beam-Restgas interactions. The validity of using this calculated geometric estimator was rigorously verified through simulation studies.

## 2. Method overview

The complete physics method consists of five stages:

1. **Generate or read an extended target profile.**
2. **Reconstruct tracks without imposing the nominal interaction point.**
3. **Estimate the interaction vertex from the track-pair POCA.**
4. **Back-propagate tracks to that vertex and perform the final vertex fit.**
5. **Correct the reconstructed $z$ distribution with a profile-dependent efficiency map.**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input target / Restgas profile rho_in(z)"]
    B["Simulation and digitization"]
    C["Apollonius displaced-track finding"]
    D["Skewed-STT z reconstruction and Kalman fit"]
    E["Initial PID without back-propagation"]
    F["p-pbar POCA vertex estimate"]
    G["Second PID with back-propagation to POCA"]
    H["Final event vertex fit"]
    I["Raw reconstructed z spectrum"]
    J["Profile-dependent MC efficiency epsilon_reco(z)"]
    K["Corrected Restgas profile"]
    L["Optional iteration with corrected profile"]

    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F --> G --> H --> I
    A --> J
    B --> J
    I --> K
    J --> K
    K --> L --> J
```

The thesis-level target workflow is **event-by-event**:

```text
raw hits
  -> Apollonius track candidates
  -> Kalman-fitted tracks
  -> PID without back-propagation
  -> event POCA
  -> reuse the original Kalman tracks
  -> PID with back-propagation to the event POCA
  -> final vertex fit
  -> reconstructed Restgas profile
```

The repository implements this event-by-event chain for both fixed-vertex and continuously distributed Restgas samples. It also provides an MC-truth control mode for closure studies.

The workflow initiates with the processing of experimental data. The raw hits from the STT are first utilized by the Apollonius algorithm to generate initial track seeds, which are subsequently refined by the Kalman Filter with hits from MVD and GEM to produce fitted trajectories. Following the tracking stage, a first PID step is performed. These preliminary tracks are then paired to analytically calculate the geometric POCA, providing the first reliable 3D estimate of the event vertex.
Crucially, the workflow then implements the POCA-First approach. Using the spatial coordinates of the determined POCA vertex as the definitive anchor, the original Kalman-fitted tracks are re-accessed and subjected to a second, targeted PID step.

Reconstruction Strategy
123
Integration with MVD and GEM (Global Tracking)
The output of the combined Apollonius and Pz Finder stages is a track seed based solely on STT information. While this seed is highly effective for identifying displaced tracks, it does not yet provide the precision required for accurate vertex reconstruction. The full integration of information from all tracking sub-detectors is therefore performed in the final Kalman filtering stage.
The Apollonius algorithm supplies an initial track candidate derived from STT isochrones, which defines a preliminary trajectory but does not include the highprecision measurements from the silicon-based detectors. These track candidates are subsequently processed by the KalmanFit using the GenFit framework, which applies a statistically rigorous Kalman filter to combine measurements from different detector systems. During this procedure, the STT-based helix is extrapolated inward toward the MVD volume, where compatible pixel or strip hits are searched for and, if found, incorporated into the track. This inward propagation significantly improves the resolution of the impact parameters 𝑑 0 and 𝑧 0 and is crucial for precisely locating the interaction vertex. In parallel, the track is extrapolated outward to the GEM stations, where additional measurements refine the momentum determination, particularly for forward-going particles, leading to an improved relative momentum resolution 𝑑𝑝/𝑝 .
As a result, the final reconstructed tracks coherently combine information from all tracking subsystems-MVD, STT, and GEM-leveraging the large acceptance and pattern recognition capability of the STT together with the superior spatial resolution of the MVD and GEM to achieve precise vertex and momentum reconstruction.
PID Step
The accurate determination of particle kinematics relies not only on precise track fitting but also on the correct association of reconstructed tracks with their physical interaction vertex during the PID step. Track candidates produced by the track finder are represented as infinite helices extending throughout the detector volume. Consequently, a crucial task of the PID step is the determination of the true physical origin of these trajectories, in order to effectively anchor and terminate them at their source. Without a well-defined starting point, essential kinematic quantities-most notably the momentum vector and the path length required for energy-loss corrections-cannot be uniquely or reliably determined.
This issue becomes particularly severe in the presence of Restgas background, where interactions occur at arbitrary locations along and within the beam pipe rather than being confined to the nominal target region. Under these conditions, the IP determination approach in the PID step must be reconsidered.
Limitations of the Standard Approach: In the standard PandaRoot workflow, a strong geometric constraint is imposed by assuming that particle trajectories originate from the beam axis near the nominal interaction point. As a result, tracks identified by the finder are processed by a Kalman Filter and typically propagated forward by ≈ 2 cm, then Kalman-fitted tracks are propagated to the point of closest approach to the 𝑧 -axis (POCA-to-line), which is then used to define the reference momentum vector and path length for the PID step.

To constrain this dominant systematic uncertainty, the investigation extended beyond software algorithms to evaluate the feasibility of a hardware-driven solution utilizing the tracking system. The study proposed the upgrade of the Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS), leveraging technology originally developed for the Luminosity Detector itself. It was demonstrated that the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS, thinned to just 50 𝜇 m, minimizes the multiple Coulomb scattering that typically degrades tracking performance at low momenta. Coupled with a fine pixel pitch of 80 × 80 𝜇 m 2 , this hardware configuration achieves a longitudinal vertex resolution of approximately 20 𝜇 m, providing the necessary sensitivity to resolve the Restgas distribution which is inaccessible to the Luminosity Detector alone. To fully exploit this hardware potential, a specialized reconstruction chain was implemented, utilizing the Apollonius triplet finder for off-IP tracking and a 'POCA-to-Point' back-propagation algorithm. This strategy optimized the reconstruction efficiency for events originating away from the nominal interaction point, allowing for the recovery of the physical density profile via a robust one-dimensional efficiency correction.
144
Summary and Outlook
The culmination of this work is the integration of the measured Restgas profile back into the luminosity determination chain, establishing a self-consistent analysis cycle. Through the implementation of a profile-dependent efficiency correction and a robust iterative workflow, the target profile with Restgas background is successfully reconstructed without the reliance on the initial model. The reconstructed profile is then used to generate an 'Effective Acceptance Map' for the luminosity fit, effectively suppressing the systematic uncertainty associated with the target profile with Restgas background to better than 0.5%. By proving that the Restgas distribution can be precisely reconstructed and accounted for, this research ensures that the deviation in the luminosity determination will not limit the PANDA experiment's ability to map the exotic hadron spectrum, thereby fulfilling the rigorous demands of next-generation hadron physics.

For instance, the final reconstructed 𝑧 -position of the interaction (after full fitting) converges to -4 . 92 cm using the POCA approach, compared to -4 . 89 cm using the MC truth value, demonstrating an excellent recovery of the event geometry. For detailed documentation of this tutorial directory, please consult web resource:

[Full Tutorial PandaRoot Analysis with Rho](http://panda-wiki.gsi.de/cgi-bin/view/Computing/PandaRootRhoTutorial)

-----------------------------

Run examples with:


## Simulation and reconstruction

    root -l -b -q tut_sim.C         # full simulation of 100 events;    ==> signal_sim.root, signal_par.root
    root -l -b -q tut_aod.C         # reconstruction of the 100 events; ==> signal_pid.root
    
    ./tut_runall.sh 100             # run both above
    
    root -l -b -q tut_fastsim.C     # fast simulation of 1000 events;   ==> signal_fast.root
    
## Analysis

    root -l -b -q tut_ana.C         # analysis of full sim events;      ==> signal_ana.root
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_fast.C    # analysis of fast sim events       ==> signal_ana_fast.root
    
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_pid.C     # analysis, PID by hand             ==> signal_ana_pid.root
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_comb.C    # analysis, combinatorics by hand   ==> signal_ana_comb.root
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_mcmatch.C # analysis, MC truth match          ==> signal_ana_mcmatch.root
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_mclist.C  # print out MC truth list infos     ==> console text output 
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_fit.C     # analysis, fitting                 ==> signal_ana_fit.root
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_ntp.C     # analysis, n-Tuple output          ==> signal_ana_ntp.root

    root -l -b -q tut_ana_compact.C # analysis compact code to ntuple;  ==> signal_ana_compact.root


## Analysis in task

-> Add line `add_subdirectory(tutorials)` in $VMCWORKDIR/CMakeLists.txt somewhere after line 260ff

    cd your/build/directory; make; cd -
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_task.C    # analysis running in a task        ==> signal_ana_task.root


## Quick analysis tools

### Running on full sim output
    root -l -b -q 'qana.C("signal_pid.root", 6.232, "J/psi->mu+ mu-;pbarpSystem->J/psi pi+ pi-", "fit4c:fitvtx:mwin(J/psi)=0.8")'    #  ==> signal_pid_ana.root
    
### Running on fast sim output
    root -l -b -q 'qana.C("signal_fast.root", 6.232, "J/psi->mu+ mu-;pbarpSystem->J/psi pi+ pi-", 0, "fit4c:fitvtx:mwin(J/psi)=0.8",1)' #  ==> signal_fast_ana.root
    
### Simulating and analysing fast simulation
    root -l -b -q 'qfsana.C("signal", "pp_jpsi2pi_jpsi_mumu.dec:pbarpSystem", 6.23, 1000, "J/psi -> mu+ mu-; pbp -> J/psi pi+ pi-", "fit4c:mwin=0.6")'     # ==> signal_0_ana.root  (1000 ev)
    root -l -b -q 'qfsana.C("bkg", "DPM", 6.232, 10000, "J/psi -> mu+ mu-; pbarpSystem -> J/psi pi+ pi-", "fit4c:fitvtx:mwin=0.8")'                        # ==> bkg_o_ana.root    (10000 ev)
    
### Submit quickfsimana jobs to virgo
    sbatch -a1-5 --chdir $PWD -- $PWD/jobquickfa_virgo.sh MySig 'qfsana.C("PREFIX","pp_jpsi2pi_jpsi_mumu.dec",7.0,1000,"J/psi->e+ e-;pbp0->J/psi pi+ pi-","fit4c:fitvtx:mwin=0.8",RUN,1)'
    sbatch -a1-5 --chdir $PWD -- $PWD/jobquickfa_virgo.sh MyBkg 'qfsana.C("PREFIX","DPM",7.0,10000,"J/psi->e+ e-;pbp0->J/psi pi+ pi-","fit4c:fitvtx:mwin=0.8",RUN,0)'

raw.text:
Preface/Requirements
*************************

This tutorial aims to demonstrate, how simulation and analysis can be performed with the PandaRoot framework. The example channel is

**p pbar ->  J/psi (-> mu+mu-) pi+ pi-**

The analysis part will cover

   * Data access
   * Particle Identification
   * Combinatorics
   * MC truth match
   * Fitting with 4 constraint (4C), vertex constraint, mass constraint

The tutorial is based on **trunk** and is meant to be an all time running tutorial. All macros and necessary files can be found under **tutorials/rho** and **macros/master**. Last test of this tutorial was done **Mar. 2022**.

Installation of PandaRoot
===========================

In order to install PandaRoot and the external packages, please follow the instructions under https://git.panda.gsi.de/PandaRootGroup/PandaRoot/-/tree/dev/docs/Installation. After installation of the libraries, you can create a folder in an arbitrary place and copy all files from ``tutorials/rho`` to this place.

General Documentation of Rho classes
======================================

There is a wiki page available under which more **detailled information about the Rho classes** is available. Please follow https://panda-wiki.gsi.de/foswiki/bin/view/Computing/PandaRootAnalysisJuly13

Files in directory tutorials/rho
==================================
All things we are going to use and run are located in the directory **tutorials/rho**.

You'll find the following files in this directory:

   * for event generation
      * ``pp_jpsi2pi_jpsi_mumu.dec`` - decay file specifying the signal decay channel

   * for running the simulation, digitization, reconstruction, and PID
      * ``tut_sim.C`` - Simulation (transport) of the generated events
      * ``tut_aod.C`` - Digitization, reconstruction and pid assignment of simulated data; this is the analysis-objects-data level (AOD).
      * ``tut_runall.sh`` - Shortcut shell script to run the two macros above for sim/digi/reco/pid macros
      * ``tut_fastsim.C`` - Run fast simulation (this skips the Geant based detailed simulation and transport, but only does smearing and acceptance cuts).
      * ``qfsana.C`` - Does fast simulation and analysis in one simple step

   * for analysis
      * ``auxtut.C`` - Some auxilliary functions for analysis
      * ``tut_ana_comb.C`` - Basic combinatorics
      * ``tut_ana_pid.C`` - Particle identification (PID)
      * ``tut_ana_mcmatch.C`` - Monte carlo truth match
      * ``tut_ana_mclist.C`` - Monte carlo truth list access
      * ``tut_ana_fit.C`` - Kinematic/vertex fitting
      * ``tut_ana.C`` - Combinatorics, PID, MC truth match and fitting all together
      * ``tut_ana_ntp.C`` - Example for using ntuple for analysis
      * ``tut_ana_fast.C`` - Does the complete analysis on the fast simulation output
      * ``qana.C`` - Simple one line macro call for a complete ntuple analysis.
      * ``tut_makegifs.C(_file_, _type_)`` - simple macro producing images with ending _type_ ("gif", "pdf", "png",...) from all histograms in _file_

   * for running analysis in a !FairTask
      * ``PndTutAnaTask.h`` - Header file of the analysis class
      * ``PndTutAnaTask.cxx`` - Source file of the analysis class
      * ``CMakeLists.txt`` - necessary to build library
      * ``tutrhoLinkDef.h`` - necessary to build library
      * ``tut_ana_task.C`` - Macro to run the analysis task
      *

Preface/Requirements
¶
This tutorial aims to demonstrate, how simulation and analysis can be performed with the PandaRoot framework. The example channel is
p pbar ->  J/psi (-> mu+mu-) pi+ pi-
The analysis part will cover
Data access
Particle Identification
Combinatorics
MC truth match
Fitting with 4 constraint (4C), vertex constraint, mass constraint
The tutorial is based on
trunk
and is meant to be an all time running tutorial. All macros and necessary files can be found under
tutorials/rho
and
macros/master
. Last test of this tutorial was done
Mar. 2022
.
Installation of PandaRoot
¶
In order to install PandaRoot and the external packages, please follow the instructions under
https://git.panda.gsi.de/PandaRootGroup/PandaRoot/-/tree/dev/docs/Installation
. After installation of the libraries, you can create a folder in an arbitrary place and copy all files from
tutorials/rho
to this place.

detailled information about the Rho classes
is available. Please follow
https://panda-wiki.gsi.de/foswiki/bin/view/Computing/PandaRootAnalysisJuly13
Files in directory tutorials/rho
¶
All things we are going to use and run are located in the directory
tutorials/rho
.
You’ll find the following files in this directory:
for event generation
pp_jpsi2pi_jpsi_mumu.dec
- decay file specifying the signal decay channel
for running the simulation, digitization, reconstruction, and PID
tut_sim.C
- Simulation (transport) of the generated events

- Digitization, reconstruction and pid assignment of simulated data; this is the analysis-objects-data level (AOD).

- Shortcut shell script to run the two macros above for sim/digi/reco/pid macros

-----------------------------

Run examples with:


## Simulation and reconstruction

    root -l -b -q tut_sim.C         # full simulation of 100 events;    ==> signal_sim.root, signal_par.root
    root -l -b -q tut_aod.C         # reconstruction of the 100 events; ==> signal_pid.root
    
    ./tut_runall.sh 100             # run both above
    
    root -l -b -q tut_fastsim.C     # fast simulation of 1000 events;   ==> signal_fast.root
    
## Analysis

    root -l -b -q tut_ana.C         # analysis of full sim events;      ==> signal_ana.root
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_fast.C    # analysis of fast sim events       ==> signal_ana_fast.root
    
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_pid.C     # analysis, PID by hand             ==> signal_ana_pid.root
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_comb.C    # analysis, combinatorics by hand   ==> signal_ana_comb.root
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_mcmatch.C # analysis, MC truth match          ==> signal_ana_mcmatch.root
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_mclist.C  # print out MC truth list infos     ==> console text output 
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_fit.C     # analysis, fitting                 ==> signal_ana_fit.root
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_ntp.C     # analysis, n-Tuple output          ==> signal_ana_ntp.root

    root -l -b -q tut_ana_compact.C # analysis compact code to ntuple;  ==> signal_ana_compact.root


## Analysis in task

-> Add line `add_subdirectory(tutorials)` in $VMCWORKDIR/CMakeLists.txt somewhere after line 260ff

    cd your/build/directory; make; cd -
    root -l -b -q tut_ana_task.C    # analysis running in a task        ==> signal_ana_task.root


## Quick analysis tools

### Running on full sim output
    root -l -b -q 'qana.C("signal_pid.root", 6.232, "J/psi->mu+ mu-;pbarpSystem->J/psi pi+ pi-", "fit4c:fitvtx:mwin(J/psi)=0.8")'    #  ==> signal_pid_ana.root
    
### Running on fast sim output
    root -l -b -q 'qana.C("signal_fast.root", 6.232, "J/psi->mu+ mu-;pbarpSystem->J/psi pi+ pi-", 0, "fit4c:fitvtx:mwin(J/psi)=0.8",1)' #  ==> signal_fast_ana.root
    
### Simulating and analysing fast simulation
    root -l -b -q 'qfsana.C("signal", "pp_jpsi2pi_jpsi_mumu.dec:pbarpSystem", 6.23, 1000, "J/psi -> mu+ mu-; pbp -> J/psi pi+ pi-", "fit4c:mwin=0.6")'     # ==> signal_0_ana.root  (1000 ev)
    root -l -b -q 'qfsana.C("bkg", "DPM", 6.232, 10000, "J/psi -> mu+ mu-; pbarpSystem -> J/psi pi+ pi-", "fit4c:fitvtx:mwin=0.8")'                        # ==> bkg_o_ana.root    (10000 ev)
    
### Submit quickfsimana jobs to virgo
    sbatch -a1-5 --chdir $PWD -- $PWD/jobquickfa_virgo.sh MySig 'qfsana.C("PREFIX","pp_jpsi2pi_jpsi_mumu.dec",7.0,1000,"J/psi->e+ e-;pbp0->J/psi pi+ pi-","fit4c:fitvtx:mwin=0.8",RUN,1)'
    sbatch -a1-5 --chdir $PWD -- $PWD/jobquickfa_virgo.sh MyBkg 'qfsana.C("PREFIX","DPM",7.0,10000,"J/psi->e+ e-;pbp0->J/psi pi+ pi-","fit4c:fitvtx:mwin=0.8",RUN,0)'

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J pndana
#SBATCH --time=8:00:00
#SBATCH --get-user-env
#SBATCH -e data/slurmlog/slurm_%j_errout.log
#SBATCH -o data/slurmlog/slurm_%j_errout.log

if [ $# -lt 1 ]; then
  echo -e "\nJob script for submission of PandaRoot analysis jobs based on macro 'prod_ana.C' on KRONOS. *The macro needs to configured beforehand!*\n"
  echo -e "   ********************************************************"  
  echo -e "   *** RECOMMENDED: Use anasub.pl for easier submission ***"  
  echo -e "   *********************************************************\n"  
  echo -e "USAGE: sbatch jobana_kronos.sh <prefix> <min> <max> <mode>\n"
  echo -e " <prefix>  : Prefix of input files"
  echo -e " <min>     : Minimum job number of files data/<prefix>_<min>_pid.root"
  echo -e " <max>     : Maximum job number of files data/<prefix>_<max>_pid.root"
  echo -e " <mode>    : Arbitrary mode number to be stored in n-tuples.\n"
  echo -e "Example : sbatch jobana_kronos.sh d0sim 1 10 42\n"
  
  exit 1
fi

nyx=$VMCWORKDIR"/macro/dayone17/fastsim"
_target=$nyx"/data/"

prefix="mysim"
from=1
to=20
mode=0

if test "$1" != ""; then
  prefix=$1
fi

if test "$2" != ""; then
  from=$2
fi

if test "$3" != ""; then
  to=$3
fi

if test "$4" != ""; then
  mode=$4
fi

echo "Running command "
echo "root -l -b -q $nyx/prod_ana.C\(\"$_target$prefix\",$from,$to,$mode\)  &> $_target$prefix""_$from""_$to""_ana.log"
root -l -b -q $nyx"/"prod_ana.C\(\"$_target$prefix\",$from,$to,$mode\)  &> $_target$prefix"_"$from"_"$to"_ana.log"

  echo -e "Example : sbatch jobana_kronos.sh d0sim 1 10 42\n"

  exit 1
fi

nyx=$VMCWORKDIR"/macro/production/scripts"

from=1

if test "$2" != ""; then

fi

6. Event Filtering for Background Events
¶
In PANDA we usually are facing a large background level of light hadronic events that we are
not interested in, where we try to identify the small fraction of interesting signal reactions,
say charmonium-like resonances. The ratio of the signal and background cross section
in this case can easily be
\(\sigma\)
sig
/
\(\sigma\)
bg
= 100nb/100mb=10
6
. In order to properly study background suppression in the analysis of the
signal channel a huge amount of background events is needed to obtain a reasonable uncertainty
on the background level estimtate.
Since doing full simulation and particle transport followed by reconstruction is a
computational expensive task a reasonable way to save computing resources is to simulate only
those background events that have a high probability to survive the initial steps of
reconstruction and selection cuts. This can be done by searching for and filtering matching
signatures already during the event generation process being overall much cheaper in terms of
computing demand.
For that purpose two event filters are existing in !PandaRoot which let the user filter on
multiplicities and invariant masses of combined candidates before the simulation stage. Please
click the links below to get documentation about these two filters.
PndFilteredPrimaryGenerator
: compact configuration with strings; complete bool logic
FairFilteredPrimaryGenerator
: configuration via different filter classes; limitations in logic

Master Macros
=============

Introduction
------------

The master macros are the standard simulation and reconstruction macros of PandaRoot. 
They use the :ref:`MasterTasks` to have the most recent default settings for the detector simulation.

Running
-------

The typical sequence of macros is:

- sim_complete.C - Event simulation. Set here the event generator you want to use
- full_complete.C - Digitization, tracking and PID in one go
- ana_complete.C - Analysis of the data. Adopt here your analysis method

A sequence which expands the digi, reco and pid ito separate steps is:

- sim_complete.C - Event simulation. Set here the event generator you want to use
- digi_complete.C - Detector response simulation and local reconstruction
- reco_complete.C - Tracking
- pid_complete.C - Combine tracks with PID information
- ana_complete.C - Analysis of the data. Adopt here your analysis method

Common User Settings
--------------------

It is encouraged that you copy the macros to a location of your choice and work from there. 
For your own analysis you have to modify the ``sim_complete.C`` macro to set the proper event generation. EvtGen mostly serves for signal events, FTF for continuum background, while the BoxGenerator is there for detector studies.
Also you have to write your own analysis. 
The ``ana_complete.C`` macro may serve as a starting point. Also the tutorial section holds many examples to draw from.

The options available in the Master Tasks can be found at :ref:`MasterTasks`.

Typically the macro flow may look like this:

.. code-block:: bash

  nEvents=1000
  geant="TGeant4"
  beammom=6.231553
  prefix="../data/myAwesomeChannel"
  options="multikalman"
  
  root -l -b q sim_complete\($nEvents,\"$geant\",$beammom,\"$prefix\",\"$options\"\)
  root -l -b q full_complete\($nEvents,\"$prefix\",\"$options\"\)
  root -l -b q ana_complete\($nEvents,\"$prefix\",\"$options\"\)

Additional Macros
-----------------

If you are interested in the output of a special stage of the simulation run or want to access a specific feature, there 
The Additional macros in this folder are:

- digiOnly_complete.C - Only does the detector simulation but not the local reconstruction
- recolocal_complete.C - Only does the local detector reconstruction.
- recoideal_complete.C - TODO
- ana_multikalman.C - Macro looking at

PandaRoot Macros
¶
Macros Folder
¶
The folder /macros contains the steering macros for PandaRoot. They are usually called via
root macroname.C
and the file name is identical to the macro name.
Most important folders are:
[master](./master/mastermacros.md):
Contains the standard macros to perform a complete simulation chain
tools:
Collection of useful macros for e.g. the event display or additional MC track information
Description of folders:
data:
Empty folder were by default the generated data of the macros is stored to
detectors:
Sub-detector specific macros
examples:
Various example macros
outdated:
Macros not used anymore
params:
Parameter files serving as an input to detector simulations
production:
Scripts and macros for larger simulation campaigns
QA:
QA macros used to test the proper running of PandaRoot
run:
Macros to run complete simulation chain with full control over the used tasks
softrig:
Macros used for the software trigger
timebased:
Macros to run time-based simulations
tracking:
Macros to run the different tracking and trackingQA algorithms
tutorials:
Tutorial macros used at various PandaRoot workshops
@ingroup group_macros
# Master Macros
These ROOT macros run a complete chain of a default PandRoot simulation. They employ the so-called Master run and Master Tasks, which are tools to provide default settings and operation modes.
It is not important where you store the macros. You may copy the whole folder to a place of your liking.
Keep in mid to source the
config.sh -p
script to set up each terminal you are using.
## First Steps
If you simply want to simulate & reconstruct some events with default settings you’ll need only 2 commands:
Starting with a simulation (here 100 events)
`
root
-l
-b
-q
sim_complete.C'(100)'
`
you may process the detector answer and reconstruction in one go:
`
root
-l
-b
-q
full_complete.C
`
and subsequently run an analysis
`
root
-l
-b
-q
full_complete.C
`
Modify the macros to suit your purpose. The sections below introduce the options.
## Output Stages
Instead of running everything in one go
`
root
-l
-b
-q
full_complete.C
`
you may run each stage separately. It is particularly useful if you want to have extra root files for each stage or if you want to stop processing at a certain stage.
`
root
-l
-b
-q
digi_complete.C
root
-l
-b
-q
reco_complete.C
root
-l
-b
-q
pid_complete.C
`
`
root
-l
-b
-q
ana_complete.C
`

Preface/Requirements
*************************

This tutorial aims to demonstrate, how simulation and analysis can be performed with the PandaRoot framework. The example channel is

**p pbar ->  J/psi (-> mu+mu-) pi+ pi-**

The analysis part will cover

   * Data access
   * Particle Identification
   * Combinatorics
   * MC truth match
   * Fitting with 4 constraint (4C), vertex constraint, mass constraint

The tutorial is based on **trunk** and is meant to be an all time running tutorial. All macros and necessary files can be found under **tutorials/rho** and **macros/master**. Last test of this tutorial was done **Mar. 2022**.

Installation of PandaRoot
===========================

In order to install PandaRoot and the external packages, please follow the instructions under https://git.panda.gsi.de/PandaRootGroup/PandaRoot/-/tree/dev/docs/Installation. After installation of the libraries, you can create a folder in an arbitrary place and copy all files from ``tutorials/rho`` to this place.

General Documentation of Rho classes
======================================

There is a wiki page available under which more **detailled information about the Rho classes** is available. Please follow https://panda-wiki.gsi.de/foswiki/bin/view/Computing/PandaRootAnalysisJuly13

Files in directory tutorials/rho
==================================
All things we are going to use and run are located in the directory **tutorials/rho**.

You'll find the following files in this directory:

   * for event generation
      * ``pp_jpsi2pi_jpsi_mumu.dec`` - decay file specifying the signal decay channel

   * for running the simulation, digitization, reconstruction, and PID
      * ``tut_sim.C`` - Simulation (transport) of the generated events
      * ``tut_aod.C`` - Digitization, reconstruction and pid assignment of simulated data; this is the analysis-objects-data level (AOD).
      * ``tut_runall.sh`` - Shortcut shell script to run the two macros above for sim/digi/reco/pid macros
      * ``tut_fastsim.C`` - Run fast simulation (this skips the Geant based detailed simulation and transport, but only does smearing and acceptance cuts).
      * ``qfsana.C`` - Does fast simulation and analysis in one simple step

   * for analysis
      * ``auxtut.C`` - Some auxilliary functions for analysis
      * ``tut_ana_comb.C`` - Basic combinatorics
      * ``tut_ana_pid.C`` - Particle identification (PID)
      * ``tut_ana_mcmatch.C`` - Monte carlo truth match
      * ``tut_ana_mclist.C`` - Monte carlo truth list access
      * ``tut_ana_fit.C`` - Kinematic/vertex fitting
      * ``tut_ana.C`` - Combinatorics, PID, MC truth match and fitting all together
      * ``tut_ana_ntp.C`` - Example for using ntuple for analysis
      * ``tut_ana_fast.C`` - Does the complete analysis on the fast simulation output
      * ``qana.C`` - Simple one line macro call for a complete ntuple analysis.
      * ``tut_makegifs.C(_file_, _type_)`` - simple macro producing images with ending _type_ ("gif", "pdf", "png",...) from all histograms in _file_

      * ``PndTutAnaTask.h`` - Header file of the analysis class
      * ``PndTutAnaTask.cxx`` - Source file of the analysis class
      * ``CMakeLists.txt`` - necessary to build library
      * ``tutrhoLinkDef.h`` - necessary to build library
      * ``tut_ana_task.C`` - Macro to run the analysis task

raw.text:
6. Event Filtering for Background Events
¶
In PANDA we usually are facing a large background level of light hadronic events that we are
not interested in, where we try to identify the small fraction of interesting signal reactions,
say charmonium-like resonances. The ratio of the signal and background cross section
in this case can easily be
\(\sigma\)
sig
/
\(\sigma\)
bg
= 100nb/100mb=10
6
. In order to properly study background suppression in the analysis of the
signal channel a huge amount of background events is needed to obtain a reasonable uncertainty
on the background level estimtate.
Since doing full simulation and particle transport followed by reconstruction is a
computational expensive task a reasonable way to save computing resources is to simulate only
those background events that have a high probability to survive the initial steps of
reconstruction and selection cuts. This can be done by searching for and filtering matching
signatures already during the event generation process being overall much cheaper in terms of
computing demand.
For that purpose two event filters are existing in !PandaRoot which let the user filter on
multiplicities and invariant masses of combined candidates before the simulation stage. Please
click the links below to get documentation about these two filters.
PndFilteredPrimaryGenerator
: compact configuration with strings; complete bool logic
FairFilteredPrimaryGenerator
: configuration via different filter classes; limitations in logic

2.5. Fitting
¶
Kinematic fitting in general is a very powerful tool in order to
improve the quality of the reconstructed objects and
reject more background.
These two things might become essential when a tiny signal has to be found in a vast amount of background. Depending on the particular analysis under consideration, there are different kinds of constraints which are the most powerful. (Example code in
tut_ana_fit.C/tut_ana.C
in the tutorial directory.)
If you want to learn more about kinematic fitting, I recommend
to read the very nice script written by Paul Avery under
http://www.phys.ufl.edu/~avery/fitting.html
.
2.5.1. Vertex Constraint
¶
Since we are dealing with decay trees, it is a very common issue, that reconstructed particles originate from a common point in space-time.
The spatial component is called vertex, and it is possible during the reconstruction of the decay tree to take advantage of this by performing a
so called
Vertex Fit
which constraints the trajectories of charged particles to come from a common point.
In our example this could be applied to the
J/psi -> mu+ mu-
decay, where the muon and anti-muon candidate have to fulfill this constraint. The fitter modifies the track parameters within errors in such a way, that the tracks come as close as possible at the hypothetical vertex. As result you get this most
probable vertex, the modified track parameters and the probability, how well the tracks meet the hypothesis.
Although vertex constraints are most powerful
for long living particles like
Lambda
or
K
S
0
, where you can e.g. require a certain distance to the IP afterwards,
we can nevertheless apply it to our
J/psi
candidate.
In PandaROOT the according classes are
RhoKalmanVtxFitter
and
RhoKinVtxFitter
, where the former is faster and the latter slightly more precise. The following code snippet shows, how those fitters can be used (both are used in the same way) based on
our
RhoCandList
from above:

...
in
event
loop
...

chi2_cut
=
...
;
//
***

vertex
fit
for
(
j

)
{
RhoKinVtxFitter
vtxfitter
(

[

]);
//

;

is

to

();
//

=

();
//

This example code shows how to access the fitted particle, the vertex and
chi
2
of the fit. When you try this example you may notice, that the
fitted mass does not differ very much from the unfitted mass. This might be due to the fact, that the
J/psi
is a very short living resonance basically decaying
in the IP, and the muons uncertainties are too large to be sufficiently incompatible with the origin.
This is the invariant mass distribution after the vertex fit (
chi
2
< 1) and the
chi
2
distribution
2.5.2. Energy-Momentum-Constraint
¶
The energy-momentum constraint fit, commonly called 4C- or 4 constraint fit, is a very powerful tool
when analyzing an exclusive decay channel, i.e. reconstructing the complete event reaction, where all
final state particles were reconstructed. In that case all components of the initial Lorentz vector
(
E, px, py, pz
):sub:
ini
have to be conserved individually. Constraining exactly that leads to
the term 4-constraint. Actually, it’s a bit of a simplification in those cases, where you want to
keep all your particles on-shell (which is usually the case for final states), which somehow adds a
couple of constraints as well.
However, there are two simple tools in PandaROOT to perform that kind of fit, that are called
Pnd4CFitter
and
PndKinFitter

raw.text:
Jupyter Notebooks
¶
Jupyter Notebooks offer a large quality of life and are becoming more important with machine learning etc. Natively PandaRoot is a collection of C++ libraries which usually are collected and called through ROOT, mostly by macros.
ROOT by itself features python bindings as well as an own C++ Kernel. With the
%%cpp
magic it is also possible to mix C++ code into python code. See the introduction to
PyROOT
.
Using the Kernels without installation
¶
It it is enough to do the following:
source <build>/config.sh -p
export JUPYTER_CONFIG_DIR=$SIMPATH/etc/root/notebook
export JUPYTER_PATH=$SIMPATH/etc/root/notebook
jupyter notebook
You now can use ROOT and PandaRoot classes in the Python3 kernel or the RootC++ kernel. Here are two example notebooks to start off with.
Examples
¶
PandaRoot Notebook Python style
Install the Kernels
¶
In some cases it is beneficial to install the Kernels to automatically be used in the system. A simple ‘jupyter notebook’ command in a fresh shell would allow them to be used. Also VSCode with the jupyter extension would be able to spawn such notebooks inside the integrated environment.
The downside is that the Kernels are pointing to one specific installation of PandaRoot and its dependencies and managing multiple installations may become cumbersome.
As a prerequisit one has to install the metakernel package in python (
pip3
install
metakernel
).
To install the Kernels simply copy the folders from
<build>/jupyter/kernels
to the appropriate place:
~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels
(Linux)
~/Library/Jupyter/kernels
(Mac)
%APPDATA%\jupyter\kernels
(Win)

ROOT by itself features python bindings as well as an own C++ Kernel. With the ``%%cpp`` magic it is also possible to mix C++ code into python code. See the introduction to PyROOT_. 

.. _PyROOT: https://root.cern.ch/notebooks/HowTos/HowTo_ROOT-Notebooks.html

Using the Kernels without installation
######################################

It it is enough to do the following::

  source <build>/config.sh -p
  export JUPYTER_CONFIG_DIR=$SIMPATH/etc/root/notebook
  export JUPYTER_PATH=$SIMPATH/etc/root/notebook
  jupyter notebook

You now can use ROOT and PandaRoot classes in the Python3 kernel or the RootC++ kernel. Here are two example notebooks to start off with.

Examples
########

.. toctree::
   :maxdepth: 2

   notebooks/PandaRootPySim
   notebooks/PandaRootCppSim

Install the Kernels
###################

In some cases it is beneficial to install the Kernels to automatically be used in the system. A simple 'jupyter notebook' command in a fresh shell would allow them to be used. Also VSCode with the jupyter extension would be able to spawn such notebooks inside the integrated environment.

The downside is that the Kernels are pointing to one specific installation of PandaRoot and its dependencies and managing multiple installations may become cumbersome.

As a prerequisit one has to install the metakernel package in python (``pip3 install metakernel``).
To install the Kernels simply copy the folders from ``<build>/jupyter/kernels`` to the appropriate place:

- ``~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels`` (Linux)
- ``~/Library/Jupyter/kernels`` (Mac)
- ``%APPDATA%\jupyter\kernels`` (Win)

raw.text:
Quick Running PandaRoot
¶
Each new shell needs to receive the proper environment variables, that PandaRoot can run. Simply load the
config.sh
which was created during the build process.
. Build/config.sh -p
Mind the space between the dot and the file name. You can provide a flag
-a
to append or
-p
to prepend to the current
PATH
and
LD_LIBRARY_PATH
variables. Appending is the least invasive to your environment, prepend is to prefer installed executables & libraries form FairSoft, FairRoot and PandaRoot. Giving no option will overwrite the environment.
Now you can call
root
, which has the appropriate version and the connection to PandaRoot. Execute any root macro, e.g:
cp -r PandaRoot/macro/master MyMacros
cd
MyMacros
root -l -b -q sim_complete
'(100, "TGeant3", 6.231552, "mytestsim")'
root -l -b -q full_complete
'(100, "mytestsim")'
In your
Build/bin
you will find a few executables, mainly some bare event generators for the use in the terminal, if necessary.

PandaRoot Macros
¶
Macros Folder
¶
The folder /macros contains the steering macros for PandaRoot. They are usually called via
root macroname.C
and the file name is identical to the macro name.
Most important folders are:
[master](./master/mastermacros.md):
Contains the standard macros to perform a complete simulation chain
tools:
Collection of useful macros for e.g. the event display or additional MC track information
Description of folders:
data:
Empty folder were by default the generated data of the macros is stored to
detectors:
Sub-detector specific macros
examples:
Various example macros
outdated:
Macros not used anymore
params:
Parameter files serving as an input to detector simulations
production:
Scripts and macros for larger simulation campaigns
QA:
QA macros used to test the proper running of PandaRoot
run:
Macros to run complete simulation chain with full control over the used tasks

# Master Macros
These ROOT macros run a complete chain of a default PandRoot simulation. They employ the so-called Master run and Master Tasks, which are tools to provide default settings and operation modes.
It is not important where you store the macros. You may copy the whole folder to a place of your liking.
Keep in mid to source the
config.sh -p
script to set up each terminal you are using.
## First Steps
If you simply want to simulate & reconstruct some events with default settings you’ll need only 2 commands:
Starting with a simulation (here 100 events)
`
root
-l
-b
-q
sim_complete.C'(100)'
`
you may process the detector answer and reconstruction in one go:
`
root
-l
-b
-q
full_complete.C
`
and subsequently run an analysis
`
root
-l
-b
-q
full_complete.C
`
Modify the macros to suit your purpose. The sections below introduce the options.
## Output Stages
Instead of running everything in one go
`
root
-l
-b
-q
full_complete.C
`
you may run each stage separately. It is particularly useful if you want to have extra root files for each stage or if you want to stop processing at a certain stage.
`
root
-l
-b
-q
digi_complete.C
root
-l
-b
-q
reco_complete.C
root
-l
-b
-q
pid_complete.C
`
`
root
-l
-b
-q
ana_complete.C
`

Master Macros
¶
Introduction
¶
The master macros are the standard simulation and reconstruction macros of PandaRoot.
They use the
MasterTasks
to have the most recent default settings for the detector simulation.
Running
¶
The typical sequence of macros is:
sim_complete.C - Event simulation. Set here the event generator you want to use
full_complete.C - Digitization, tracking and PID in one go
ana_complete.C - Analysis of the data. Adopt here your analysis method
A sequence which expands the digi, reco and pid ito separate steps is:
sim_complete.C - Event simulation. Set here the event generator you want to use
digi_complete.C - Detector response simulation and local reconstruction
reco_complete.C - Tracking
pid_complete.C - Combine tracks with PID information
ana_complete.C - Analysis of the data. Adopt here your analysis method
Common User Settings
¶
It is encouraged that you copy the macros to a location of your choice and work from there.
For your own analysis you have to modify the
sim_complete.C
macro to set the proper event generation. EvtGen mostly serves for signal events, FTF for continuum background, while the BoxGenerator is there for detector studies.
Also you have to write your own analysis.
The
ana_complete.C
macro may serve as a starting point. Also the tutorial section holds many examples to draw from.
The options available in the Master Tasks can be found at
MasterTasks
.

Jupyter Notebooks
¶
Jupyter Notebooks offer a large quality of life and are becoming more important with machine learning etc. Natively PandaRoot is a collection of C++ libraries which usually are collected and called through ROOT, mostly by macros.
ROOT by itself features python bindings as well as an own C++ Kernel. With the
%%cpp
magic it is also possible to mix C++ code into python code. See the introduction to
PyROOT
.
Using the Kernels without installation
¶
It it is enough to do the following:
source <build>/config.sh -p
export JUPYTER_CONFIG_DIR=$SIMPATH/etc/root/notebook
export JUPYTER_PATH=$SIMPATH/etc/root/notebook
jupyter notebook
You now can use ROOT and PandaRoot classes in the Python3 kernel or the RootC++ kernel. Here are two example notebooks to start off with.
Examples
¶
PandaRoot Notebook Python style
Install the Kernels
¶
In some cases it is beneficial to install the Kernels to automatically be used in the system. A simple ‘jupyter notebook’ command in a fresh shell would allow them to be used. Also VSCode with the jupyter extension would be able to spawn such notebooks inside the integrated environment.
The downside is that the Kernels are pointing to one specific installation of PandaRoot and its dependencies and managing multiple installations may become cumbersome.
As a prerequisit one has to install the metakernel package in python (
pip3
install
metakernel
).
To install the Kernels simply copy the folders from
<build>/jupyter/kernels
to the appropriate place:
~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels
(Linux)
~/Library/Jupyter/kernels
(Mac)
%APPDATA%\jupyter\kernels
(Win)

=================

Jupyter Notebooks offer a large quality of life and are becoming more important with machine learning etc. Natively PandaRoot is a collection of C++ libraries which usually are collected and called through ROOT, mostly by macros.

ROOT by itself features python bindings as well as an own C++ Kernel. With the ``%%cpp`` magic it is also possible to mix C++ code into python code. See the introduction to PyROOT_. 

.. _PyROOT: https://root.cern.ch/notebooks/HowTos/HowTo_ROOT-Notebooks.html

Using the Kernels without installation
######################################

It it is enough to do the following::

  source <build>/config.sh -p
  export JUPYTER_CONFIG_DIR=$SIMPATH/etc/root/notebook
  export JUPYTER_PATH=$SIMPATH/etc/root/notebook
  jupyter notebook

You now can use ROOT and PandaRoot classes in the Python3 kernel or the RootC++ kernel. Here are two example notebooks to start off with.

Examples
########

.. toctree::
   :maxdepth: 2

   notebooks/PandaRootPySim
   notebooks/PandaRootCppSim

Install the Kernels
###################

In some cases it is beneficial to install the Kernels to automatically be used in the system. A simple 'jupyter notebook' command in a fresh shell would allow them to be used. Also VSCode with the jupyter extension would be able to spawn such notebooks inside the integrated environment.

The downside is that the Kernels are pointing to one specific installation of PandaRoot and its dependencies and managing multiple installations may become cumbersome.

As a prerequisit one has to install the metakernel package in python (``pip3 install metakernel``).
To install the Kernels simply copy the folders from ``<build>/jupyter/kernels`` to the appropriate place:

- ``~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels`` (Linux)
- ``~/Library/Jupyter/kernels`` (Mac)
- ``%APPDATA%\jupyter\kernels`` (Win)

pip
install
