raw.text:
Building the documentation
==========================

Prerequisites
-------------

The documentation system of PandaRoot relies on two different external programs.
The first one is `doxygen <https://www.doxygen.nl/index.html>`_ which is used to extract the comments written in the source files to generate an API documentation.
The second external program is `sphinx <https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/>`_ which is used to generate a nice looking webpage which contains also the manuals written in the docs folder.
Sphinx uses in addition `breathe <https://breathe.readthedocs.io/en/latest/>`_ which allows to incorporate the doxygen generated documentation into the sphinx web-pages.
For Sphinx to work you need to have `python3 <https://www.python.org/>`_ installed in your system.

**Doxygen**

You can grab the files to install doxygen from the `official download page <https://www.doxygen.nl/download.html>`_ and install it.

**Sphinx**

The `official instructions <https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/installation.html>`_ offer different ways for installation.
Take the one you prefer.

**Read the Docs Sphinx Theme**

The PandaRoot documentation uses the "Read the Docs" theme which has to be installed via pip:
::
  
  pip install sphinx_rtd_theme


**Breathe**

Breathe is the bridge between doxygen and Sphinx and can be installed via pip:
::

  pip install breathe

**MyST parser**

MyST is the bridge between md files and Sphinx and can be installed via pip:
::

  pip install myst-parser

**Notebook Rendering**

The package nbsphinx will render Jupyter notebooks to html:
::

  pip install nbsphinx

**Graphviz**

`Graphviz <https://graphviz.org/>`_ can be used by Sphinx for plotting.

Generating the documentation
----------------------------

The documentation can be created via two cmake calls.
The first creates the doxygen documentation:
::

  cmake --build ./build --target doxygen

The second one creates the sphinx part of the documentation:
::
  
  cmake --build ./build --target sphinx

The output is stored in ``<build_folder>/docs/doxygen`` resp. ``<build_folder>/docs/sphinx``.
Opening the ``index.html`` file in one of the folders with an html browser shows the start page of the documentation.


Sphinx in Visual Studio Code 
----------------------------

VS Code is a free integrated development platform which offers many extensions and can handle git, cmake, c++, python, jupyter notebooks and even rudimentary root file access. 

Also for our documentation you may use VS Code to create a quick preview of what you are editing. After installing spinx etc. like above you can install in VS Code the "Extension Pack for reStructuredText" and subsequently some dependencies (e.g. esbonio language server) announced by the notification pop-ups. The preview can be opened by a button at the top right corner of the file editor tab.

The ``.rst`` file you're editing has to be stored in our ``docs/`` folder and should be included in a table of content. The artifacts, i.e. the ``index.html`` to check links in a browser, can be found then in ``docs/_build/`` by default.

VS Code is a free integrated development platform which offers many extensions and can handle git, cmake, c++, python, jupyter notebooks and even rudimentary root file access.
If you want to build PandaRoot with VS Code you should install a few extensions first. Most important are “C/C++” and “C/C++ Themes” as well as “CMake” and “CMake Tools”.
It is recommended to tweak the CMake tool settings to build somewhere else than the default location (<source>/build/) in the “Cmake: Build Directory” setting. Also you may want to set the correct environment variables to the FairRoot & FairSoft installations in the “Cmake: Build Environment” and “Cmake: Configure Environment”. This may not be necessary if your shell profile or bashrc already set these.
You can load your source directory in a fresh workspace (don’t forget to save it as a workspace) and then make use of cmake and/or building e.g. from the bottom bar of the application.
Also VS Code comes built-in with an easy way to manage and review your changes with git.
A very useful extension is “clangd”, which enables a lot of features to improve code navigation and much more. You have to add an additional the build argument
-DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=1
in your Cmake extension settings. Then symlink the file
compile_commands.json
from your build directory to your source directory.

raw.text:
Prerequisites
¶
The documentation system of PandaRoot relies on two different external programs.
The first one is
doxygen
which is used to extract the comments written in the source files to generate an API documentation.
The second external program is
sphinx
which is used to generate a nice looking webpage which contains also the manuals written in the docs folder.
Sphinx uses in addition
breathe
which allows to incorporate the doxygen generated documentation into the sphinx web-pages.
For Sphinx to work you need to have
python3
installed in your system.
Doxygen
You can grab the files to install doxygen from the
official download page
and install it.
Sphinx
The
official instructions
offer different ways for installation.
Take the one you prefer.
Read the Docs Sphinx Theme
The PandaRoot documentation uses the “Read the Docs” theme which has to be installed via pip:
pip
install
sphinx_rtd_theme
Breathe
Breathe is the bridge between doxygen and Sphinx and can be installed via pip:
pip
install
breathe
MyST parser
MyST is the bridge between md files and Sphinx and can be installed via pip:
pip
install
myst
-
parser
Notebook Rendering
The package nbsphinx will render Jupyter notebooks to html:
pip
install
nbsphinx
Graphviz
Graphviz
can be used by Sphinx for plotting.

raw.text:
Installation process
¶
First you need to set the environment variables SIMPATH and FAIRROOTPATH, which are the folders where you have the installed the external packages and FairRoot. If the installation was done with Spack, both folders may be the same. On a cluster this may be already pre-installed for you, e.g. on a CVMFS.
export
FAIRROOTPATH
=
/home/pandauser/FairRoot-vXX.X/install
export
SIMPATH
=
/home/pandauser/fairsoft_XXX/build/
If you are at a GSI machine, you should have access to the CVMFS. You can find Installations of FairSoft and FairRoot at
/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de
. Mind the correct operating system.
Build PandaRoot
¶
Create a build directory and build the sources (here in ../source):
mkdir build
cd
build
cmake ../source
make -j4
You can change the
-j4
to the number of CPU cores you have available to speed up the process.
If your CMake installation on your system is too old, then the external packages installed a new one. You can use this line instead:
$SIMPATH
/bin/cmake ../PandaRoot
To setup PandaRoot in a new shell, just source the configuration script:
. build/config.sh -a
You can provide a flag -a to append or -p to prepend to the current PATH and LD_LIBRARY_PATH variables. Appending is the least invasive to your environment, prepend is to prefer installed executables & libraries form FairSoft, FairRoot and PandaRoot. Giving no option will overwrite the environment.
Out-of-build installation
¶
There is the possibility to copy the build products into an installation folder, which allows to delete the build and source folders. You need to provide the installation folder at the configuration stage, build and install:
mkdir build
mkdir install
cd
build
cmake -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX
=
../install ../PandaRoot
make -j4
make install
You will find all the necessary input and parameter files in
install/share
. In order to load PandaRoot in a shell you need to source the configuration from here:
. install/bin/config.sh -p
Build with Visual Studio Code
¶
VS Code is a free integrated development platform which offers many extensions and can handle git, cmake, c++, python, jupyter notebooks and even rudimentary root file access.
If you want to build PandaRoot with VS Code you should install a few extensions first. Most important are “C/C++” and “C/C++ Themes” as well as “CMake” and “CMake Tools”.
It is recommended to tweak the CMake tool settings to build somewhere else than the default location (<source>/build/) in the “Cmake: Build Directory” setting. Also you may want to set the correct environment variables to the FairRoot & FairSoft installations in the “Cmake: Build Environment” and “Cmake: Configure Environment”. This may not be necessary if your shell profile or bashrc already set these.
You can load your source directory in a fresh workspace (don’t forget to save it as a workspace) and then make use of cmake and/or building e.g. from the bottom bar of the application.
Also VS Code comes built-in with an easy way to manage and review your changes with git.
A very useful extension is “clangd”, which enables a lot of features to improve code navigation and much more. You have to add an additional the build argument
-DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=1
in your Cmake extension settings. Then symlink the file
compile_commands.json
from your build directory to your source directory.

Running PandaRoot
¶
Contents:
Running Sequence
Event Generator
Transport
Digitizer
Reconstruction
MasterTasks
Simulations Macro
Digitization/Reconstruction Macro
Using the Logger from Fair
Usage inside the Code
Options in a ROOT macro
Running the software encloses a lot of algorithms and packages. A comprehensive overview is given in
Running Sequence
. For a quick way to set up everything it is recommended to familiarize with the
MasterTasks
. Developers also should have a look at the useful logging possibilities in
Using the Logger from Fair
.
Event Generation
¶
First stage is the event generation. It simulates the interaction of the antiproton beam with the target.
It does not include any interaction with the PANDA detector which is important for the decay of long living charged particles like hyperons.
Transport
¶
In the second stage the particles generated via the event generator are transported through the detector. This is done via either
Geant3
or
Geant4
which can be seamlessly selected via
VMC
.
In this stage the particle properties like their decay length, interaction with the detector material and fields are taken into account.
It creates a realistic picture about the processes taking place inside the detector. The output of this stage is
a Monte Carlo truth list of generated particles with their point of origin, momentum, charge and creation time, and, for each sub-detector, a list
of points where the particles have interacted with sensitive detector material, containing the time, position and lost energy at that point.
Digitization
¶
In the digitization stage the detector responds to the deposited charge in the sensitive volume is simulated.
In contains both the sensor properties as well as the readout electronics features of a subdetector.
The output should be a data stream matching with the one generated by the DAQ of the real PANDA experiment.
What is simulated and how detailed the simulation is, differs for each sub-detector.
Reconstruction
¶
The reconstruction is subdivided into two stages, the local reconstruction and the global reconstruction.
Local Reconstruction
¶
The local reconstruction is operating on the sub-detector data independently from each other and is part of the sub-detector code.
It translates the digitized detector data back into physical quantities like the translation from fired detector channel into a position in the detector,
or an ADC value back into an energy.
Global Reconstruction/Tracking
¶
Global reconstruction in PANDA mainly means reconstructing the track of charged particles from the measured hit points in the tracking detector.
This process happens again in two stages. The firs one is the track finding and pre-fitting stage. Here the hit points are sorted into
groups of hits which could belong to one track and a rough estimate of the track parameters like charge, momentum and position on track are calculated.
In the second stage a Kalman filter is used to improve the track parameters by taking also energy loss and multiple scattering into account
which is typically neglected in the pre-fitting stage.
Particle Identification
¶
The last stage before the analysis is the particle identification (PID). Here the tracks of the global reconstruction are combined with the measurements
of the PID detectors and the EMC and a probability for each stable particle species is calculated (e, pi, mu, K, p).
The complete information about one particle is then stored in a charged candidate. For those cluster in the EMC where no track is pointing to
an addition neutral candidate is created.
Analysis
¶
A analysis of a simulated physics channel or background data is performed using the Rho package.

The PandaRoot framework incorporates a modular design approach, where each subsystem is allocated its own package for Monte Carlo processing, digitization, reconstruction, tracking and particle identification (PID). The detector components within each subsystem employ unique algorithms to compute the probability density function (PDF) for each particle hypothesis. The combination of the PDFs from all detector components is accomplished through the use of a Bayesian approach, resulting in a global likelihood for PID.
Upon completion of data flow, the PandaRoot framework offers a range of algorithms for the tracking and particle identification, in addition to comprehensive analysis tools including the 𝑅ℎ𝑜 package and the kinematic fitter package. The latter package facilitates a range of fitting techniques, including vertex fitting, mass constraint fitting, 4C Kinematic fitting, and decay tree fitting. The Rho package provides a unique mechanism for consolidating particle candidate lists, which effectively eliminates the potential for double counting through the use of indexed candidates. Additionally, the package includes support for PID, tracking, and generated Monte Carlo information, further enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of the physics analysis process.

raw.text: ¯ PANDA trigger and DAQ Because the high precision physics goals of the ¯ PANDA experiment require a substantial amount of data, the ¯ PANDA data acquisition (DAQ) system has to handle high data rates of up to 200 GB/ sec at an average interaction rate of 20 MHz [ 88 ]. To deal with the large fraction of background a sophisticated event filtering and trigger system are mandatory. One unique feature of ¯ PANDA is that no global hardware trigger will be used, but instead solely a partial reconstruction of the events will lead to the trigger decision. Every detector front end is running independently and employs feature extraction algorithms to select relevant data. It is collected by data concentrators and sent to a two stage event building network. Compute nodes reconstruct the reactions on the fly in order to form a trigger decision and write the interesting events to tape. To synchronize the DAQ system across all sub-detectors the synchronization of data acquisition (SODA) protocol[ 89 ] will be used. It offers a global clock with a jitter of less than 20 ps and timestamps coupled to the HESR beam structure. This way it is possible to assemble a complete event out of the information from individual detector components within the event building network.

What is simulated and how detailed the simulation is, differs for each sub-detector.
Reconstruction
¶
The reconstruction is subdivided into two stages, the local reconstruction and the global reconstruction.
Local Reconstruction
¶
The local reconstruction is operating on the sub-detector data independently from each other and is part of the sub-detector code.
It translates the digitized detector data back into physical quantities like the translation from fired detector channel into a position in the detector,
or an ADC value back into an energy.
Global Reconstruction/Tracking
¶
Global reconstruction in PANDA mainly means reconstructing the track of charged particles from the measured hit points in the tracking detector.
This process happens again in two stages. The firs one is the track finding and pre-fitting stage. Here the hit points are sorted into
groups of hits which could belong to one track and a rough estimate of the track parameters like charge, momentum and position on track are calculated.
In the second stage a Kalman filter is used to improve the track parameters by taking also energy loss and multiple scattering into account
which is typically neglected in the pre-fitting stage.
Particle Identification
¶
The last stage before the analysis is the particle identification (PID). Here the tracks of the global reconstruction are combined with the measurements
of the PID detectors and the EMC and a probability for each stable particle species is calculated (e, pi, mu, K, p).
The complete information about one particle is then stored in a charged candidate. For those cluster in the EMC where no track is pointing to
an addition neutral candidate is created.
Analysis
¶
A analysis of a simulated physics channel or background data is performed using the Rho package.

Event Generation
¶

It does not include any interaction with the PANDA detector which is important for the decay of long living charged particles like hyperons.
Transport
¶
In the second stage the particles generated via the event generator are transported through the detector. This is done via either

or
Geant4
which can be seamlessly selected via

It creates a realistic picture about the processes taking place inside the detector. The output of this stage is
a Monte Carlo truth list of generated particles with their point of origin, momentum, charge and creation time, and, for each sub-detector, a list
of points where the particles have interacted with sensitive detector material, containing the time, position and lost energy at that point.

Upon completion of data flow, the PandaRoot framework offers a range of algorithms for the tracking and particle identification, in addition to comprehensive analysis tools including the 𝑅ℎ𝑜 package and the kinematic fitter package. The latter package facilitates a range of fitting techniques, including vertex fitting, mass constraint fitting, 4C Kinematic fitting, and decay tree fitting. The Rho package provides a unique mechanism for consolidating particle candidate lists, which effectively eliminates the potential for double counting through the use of indexed candidates. Additionally, the package includes support for PID, tracking, and generated Monte Carlo information, further enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of the physics analysis process.
48
The PANDA Experiment at FAIR
Figure 2.16: Structure of FairRoot. External libraries at the top, the framework in the middle and the special experiments at the bottom. Figure adapted from [112].
Figure 2.17: Scheme of PandaRoot data flow. Figure adapted from [107].
The Silicon Detector Software (SDS) is a specialized, highly integrated software package designed for all silicon detector components within the PANDA experiment, including MVD and LMD. By utilizing C++ inheritance mechanisms, the SDS significantly simplifies the development and maintenance of software packages intended for individual silicon sub-detectors. The SDS interfaces seamlessly with PandaRoot through the FairTask mechanism, which orchestrates the entire data processing and analysis workflow. Conceptually, the SDS workflow proceeds sequentially through two principal phases: Monte-Carlo transport coupled with electronic digitization, followed by hit reconstruction and clustering.

A comprehensive schematic structure of FairRoot is presented in Figure 2.16. As explicitly illustrated, the software architecture is intrinsically divided into three hierarchical layers: the underlying dependencies (top), the core framework (middle), and the experiment-specific implementations (bottom). The top layer comprises the foundational ROOT libraries and the Virtual Monte Carlo (VMC) [115] interface. Developed at CERN, ROOT provides a vast array of tools essential for high-energy physics, encompassing robust data analysis and performance simulation functionalities, thereby serving as the absolute bedrock of FairRoot. Working together with ROOT is the VMC, a widely utilized abstraction tool in high-energy physics. The VMC enables seamless access to various Monte Carlo transport engines without necessitating any alterations to the user's code, geometry, or detector descriptions. Presently, VMC supports the use of both GEANT3 [116] and GEANT4 [117], with support for FLUKA [118] currently under development. GEANT itself is the standard application suite for simulating the passage of particles through matter. It exists in two major iterations: GEANT3, which is a legacy system coded in FORTRAN, and GEANT4, a modern evolution written in C++ that employs an object-oriented design to implement physics processes more generally. Because the simulation results produced by GEANT3 and GEANT4 are nearly identical for many standard applications, both versions remain extensively employed and validated within the high-energy physics community. The middle layer constitutes the FairRoot core, which centrally manages the execution flow through the Run Manager. On one hand, the framework delivers managing classes that drive the execution of a simulation or reconstruction session, handle the Input/Output (I/O) to files, process parameter I/O, and build the geometry for a simulation from various input files. On the other hand, it provides essential base classes for detector handling, magnetic field definition, event generators for simulation sessions, and base task structures used for analysis sessions. Finally, the bottom layer contains the experiment-specific code. Historically, the code base was split into the base part called FairRoot and the experiment-specific parts, such as CbmRoot and PandaRoot. In this bottom tier, individual PANDA sub-detectors (e.g., MVD, STT, EMC) and their distinct digitization or track-finding algorithms are securely implemented by inheriting from the middle-layer core base classes. Using and extending the task mechanism of ROOT, it is possible to implement complex analysis tasks in a highly structured manner. Within this framework, FairTask serves as the fundamental class that facilitates the construction of a hierarchical tree of processing tasks. Derived from ROOT's base TTask class, it can elegantly contain multiple sub-tasks that are executed recursively. Consequently, highly sophisticated simulation and reconstruction programs can be dynamically assembled and executed simply by invoking the services of the top-level task or its specific sub-tasks.
The PandaRoot Software
47
Figure 2.17 depicts the data flow of the PandaRoot framework. The simulation process involves the generation of physics and background events using several event generators such as 'Particle Gun', EvtGen, DPM, PYTHIA, and UrQMD. The VMC is utilized for the transportation of the generated particles through the detectors, where they interact with the sensitive elements. The energy deposit resulting from these interactions is digitized to simulate future measurements of the experiments. Using the digitized output of the sinulation or experiment data, the hits can be reconstructed, followed by track finding, fitting, and particle identification to perform the physics analysis.

# PandaRoot

This software is designed to the specific needs of the PANDA experiment. It is used to perform event generation, particle transport ("simulation"), detector digitisation and reconstruction, particle identification as well as event analysis.

(Virtual Monte-Carlo [60]), ROOT (Plotting, ﬁtting, graphics etc. [61]), Pythia [62]
and auxiliary tools
• FairRoot handling the framework (data I/O, interfaces, infrastructure). The task
is to provide all steps of the data processing up to the physics analysis stage.
Data is stored in a ROOT ﬁle, using ROOT objects handling with chains, trees and
branches.
• DetectorRoot detector framework (detector simulations and data reconstruction).
For the Panda experiment such framework is called PandaRoot.
The PandaRoot framework user should add detector class implementations for the
transport model and reconstruction tasks, which are processing the data. A typical chain
of generating and processing of simulated data contains the following ingredients:
1. Event Generator:
The event generator produces in each event a set of particles according to the in-
vestigated physics reaction or detector studies. Particles are deﬁned by their type
and four-momentum, point of origin and time. Those properties are randomly
distributed by the selected model. In PandaRoot for this purpose several gener-
ators are available. The "BOX" generator provides a uniform distribution for all
variables. It also has possibility to choose a certain variable range. A generator
for single-channel generation is called EvtGen [63]. And the DPM [64] generator
provides the full description of all antiproton-proton reactions.
2. Transport Code (VMC):
The particle transport through matter is simulated by Geant [58],[59]. The Virtual
Monte-Carlo interface (VMC) allows to switch between the diﬀerent Geant ver-
sions as well as to introduce other packages. Each sub-detector has its own geom-
etry description (usually in ROOT format) and deﬁnition of the active and passive
elements. For all materials in which particles can interact according to physical
processes, such as ionization, showering or Cherenkov emission, they react with
the detector material and loss of energy is estimated. Interaction of particle with
the detector material (e.g position and energy loss) is saved in each event. This
data is called MCHits and it is accessible for the analysis of the performance of
the reconstruction steps.
3. Digitization:
All Monte-Carlo data is processed to model the detectors response. The threshold,
eﬃciency and ampliﬁcation can be adjusted according to the measurements of
real detector response. The digitized data formats in the simulation must be the
same as those obtained in a real implementation (a prototype detector or even
the ﬁnal setup). This data is called DigiHits and is used as input information for
reconstruction of the events.

raw.text: ¯ PANDA trigger and DAQ Because the high precision physics goals of the ¯ PANDA experiment require a substantial amount of data, the ¯ PANDA data acquisition (DAQ) system has to handle high data rates of up to 200 GB/ sec at an average interaction rate of 20 MHz [ 88 ]. To deal with the large fraction of background a sophisticated event filtering and trigger system are mandatory. One unique feature of ¯ PANDA is that no global hardware trigger will be used, but instead solely a partial reconstruction of the events will lead to the trigger decision. Every detector front end is running independently and employs feature extraction algorithms to select relevant data. It is collected by data concentrators and sent to a two stage event building network. Compute nodes reconstruct the reactions on the fly in order to form a trigger decision and write the interesting events to tape. To synchronize the DAQ system across all sub-detectors the synchronization of data acquisition (SODA) protocol[ 89 ] will be used. It offers a global clock with a jitter of less than 20 ps and timestamps coupled to the HESR beam structure. This way it is possible to assemble a complete event out of the information from individual detector components within the event building network.

Running the software encloses a lot of algorithms and packages. A comprehensive overview is given in
Running Sequence
. For a quick way to set up everything it is recommended to familiarize with the
MasterTasks
. Developers also should have a look at the useful logging possibilities in
Using the Logger from Fair
.
Event Generation
¶
First stage is the event generation. It simulates the interaction of the antiproton beam with the target.
It does not include any interaction with the PANDA detector which is important for the decay of long living charged particles like hyperons.
Transport
¶
In the second stage the particles generated via the event generator are transported through the detector. This is done via either
Geant3
or
Geant4
which can be seamlessly selected via
VMC
.
In this stage the particle properties like their decay length, interaction with the detector material and fields are taken into account.
It creates a realistic picture about the processes taking place inside the detector. The output of this stage is
a Monte Carlo truth list of generated particles with their point of origin, momentum, charge and creation time, and, for each sub-detector, a list
of points where the particles have interacted with sensitive detector material, containing the time, position and lost energy at that point.
Digitization
¶
In the digitization stage the detector responds to the deposited charge in the sensitive volume is simulated.
In contains both the sensor properties as well as the readout electronics features of a subdetector.
The output should be a data stream matching with the one generated by the DAQ of the real PANDA experiment.
What is simulated and how detailed the simulation is, differs for each sub-detector.
Reconstruction
¶
The reconstruction is subdivided into two stages, the local reconstruction and the global reconstruction.
Local Reconstruction
¶
The local reconstruction is operating on the sub-detector data independently from each other and is part of the sub-detector code.
It translates the digitized detector data back into physical quantities like the translation from fired detector channel into a position in the detector,
or an ADC value back into an energy.
Global Reconstruction/Tracking
¶
Global reconstruction in PANDA mainly means reconstructing the track of charged particles from the measured hit points in the tracking detector.
This process happens again in two stages. The firs one is the track finding and pre-fitting stage. Here the hit points are sorted into
groups of hits which could belong to one track and a rough estimate of the track parameters like charge, momentum and position on track are calculated.
In the second stage a Kalman filter is used to improve the track parameters by taking also energy loss and multiple scattering into account
which is typically neglected in the pre-fitting stage.
Particle Identification
¶
The last stage before the analysis is the particle identification (PID). Here the tracks of the global reconstruction are combined with the measurements
of the PID detectors and the EMC and a probability for each stable particle species is calculated (e, pi, mu, K, p).
The complete information about one particle is then stored in a charged candidate. For those cluster in the EMC where no track is pointing to
an addition neutral candidate is created.
Analysis
¶
A analysis of a simulated physics channel or background data is performed using the Rho package.

raw.text:
The PandaRoot framework incorporates a modular design approach, where each subsystem is allocated its own package for Monte Carlo processing, digitization, reconstruction, tracking and particle identification (PID). The detector components within each subsystem employ unique algorithms to compute the probability density function (PDF) for each particle hypothesis. The combination of the PDFs from all detector components is accomplished through the use of a Bayesian approach, resulting in a global likelihood for PID.
Upon completion of data flow, the PandaRoot framework offers a range of algorithms for the tracking and particle identification, in addition to comprehensive analysis tools including the 𝑅ℎ𝑜 package and the kinematic fitter package. The latter package facilitates a range of fitting techniques, including vertex fitting, mass constraint fitting, 4C Kinematic fitting, and decay tree fitting. The Rho package provides a unique mechanism for consolidating particle candidate lists, which effectively eliminates the potential for double counting through the use of indexed candidates. Additionally, the package includes support for PID, tracking, and generated Monte Carlo information, further enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of the physics analysis process.

The Silicon Detector Software (SDS) is a specialized, highly integrated software package designed for all silicon detector components within the PANDA experiment, including MVD and LMD. By utilizing C++ inheritance mechanisms, the SDS significantly simplifies the development and maintenance of software packages intended for individual silicon sub-detectors. The SDS interfaces seamlessly with PandaRoot through the FairTask mechanism, which orchestrates the entire data processing and analysis workflow. Conceptually, the SDS workflow proceeds sequentially through two principal phases: Monte-Carlo transport coupled with electronic digitization, followed by hit reconstruction and clustering.
The PandaRoot Software
49
To accurately simulate the physical processes, the detector geometry is first meticulously modeled based on the ROOT framework, organized as a hierarchical nesting of volumes called assemblies. The basic physical volumes are translated and rotated to form these higher-level assemblies. Because the tree of assemblies is accessed via a directory of their names, identifying specific sensors requires a full structural path. To streamline this process during data processing, the PndGeoHandling class is utilized to dynamically map the sensitive physical volumes to unique integer identifiers known as sensor IDs. Furthermore, to optimize computational performance, only interactions within predefined active volumes (e.g., designated by names like 'PixelActive') are evaluated and stored.
The data processing pipeline, illustrated in detail in Figure 2.18, begins with MonteCarlo Transport and Digitization . Primary particles generated by event generators are propagated through the detector geometry and magnetic field via the Virtual Monte Carlo (VMC) interface (utilizing engines like GEANT3 or GEANT4). Whenever a simulated particle traverses an active silicon volume managed by PndSdsDetector , a Monte-Carlo point ( SdsMCPoint ) is instantiated. This point records crucial exact physical quantities, including the entry and exit coordinates, momentum, energy loss within the volume, and the precise time of flight.
Subsequently, the SdsHitProducer executes the digitization process. Digitization simulates the specific electronic response of the detector, converting the continuous energy loss of the SdsMCPoint into discrete digital signals ( SdsDigi , specialized as PndSdsDigiPixel or PndSdsDigiStrip ). Depending on the sensor thickness and technological properties, the SDS package employs different physical models to distribute the deposited charge across the readout channels:
Linear Model: For ultra-thin silicon sensors, such as the 50 𝜇 m thick HV-MAPS, the particle trajectory within the sensor bulk is sufficiently short to be approximated as a straight line. The deposited charge is assumed to be uniformly distributed along this projected track. Therefore, the charge 𝑄 𝑖 measured by each strip 𝑖 , or 𝑄 𝑖,𝑗 measured by each pixel ( 𝑖, 𝑗 ), is determined geometrically:
where 𝑄 is the total deposited charge, ( 𝑥 𝑖𝑛 , 𝑦 𝑖𝑛 ) and ( 𝑥 𝑜𝑢𝑡 , 𝑦 𝑜𝑢𝑡 ) are the entry and exit coordinates of the track inside the sensor volume, and the subscripted coordinates represent the entry and exit points within the specific pitch or pixel boundaries.
Static Charge Cloud Model: Conversely, for thicker sensors, such as the 200 𝜇 m hybrid pixel sensors, the drifting charge carriers experience significant lateral diffusion, rendering the straight-line approximation inadequate. Chapter4
Extraction of the luminosity
For the determination of the luminosity, the diﬀerential cross section in dependence of
the scattering angle has to be extracted from data. The data reconstruction includes
several necessary steps: ﬁnding and ﬁtting of the tracks of the elastically scattered
antiprotons and backtracking them to the interaction point in order to get rid of the
inﬂuence of the magnetic ﬁeld.
A complete simulation of the PANDA detector components and their response to
the passage of particles has been developed within the PandaRoot framework [57]. It
is designed that way that the same reconstruction and analysis algorithms will work on
the simulation output as well as on data. This chapter gives an overview of the frame-
work and describes all procedures related to the track reconstruction in the luminosity
detector and related performance studies.
4.1
PandaRoot framework layout
The software framework is a collection of software packages and tools for the descrip-
tion of the single detector components and the simulation of physics reactions. The
layout is organized such as to allow the re-use of well known programs and tools, com-
mon to particle and nuclear physics simulations. One basic concept of the framework
is its modularity, the possibility to switch algorithms and procedures at any point in
the chain of processes. Hence a set of interfaces and data input/output are provided to
connect all these tools properly.
Almost all experiments at the future FAIR facility are using the following features of
organization of their software packages:
• External Packages with the commonly used packages as Geant3 and Geant4 (prop-
agation of particles through matter written in Fortran [58] and C++ [59]), VMC

A comprehensive schematic structure of FairRoot is presented in Figure 2.16. As explicitly illustrated, the software architecture is intrinsically divided into three hierarchical layers: the underlying dependencies (top), the core framework (middle), and the experiment-specific implementations (bottom). The top layer comprises the foundational ROOT libraries and the Virtual Monte Carlo (VMC) [115] interface. Developed at CERN, ROOT provides a vast array of tools essential for high-energy physics, encompassing robust data analysis and performance simulation functionalities, thereby serving as the absolute bedrock of FairRoot. Working together with ROOT is the VMC, a widely utilized abstraction tool in high-energy physics. The VMC enables seamless access to various Monte Carlo transport engines without necessitating any alterations to the user's code, geometry, or detector descriptions. Presently, VMC supports the use of both GEANT3 [116] and GEANT4 [117], with support for FLUKA [118] currently under development. GEANT itself is the standard application suite for simulating the passage of particles through matter. It exists in two major iterations: GEANT3, which is a legacy system coded in FORTRAN, and GEANT4, a modern evolution written in C++ that employs an object-oriented design to implement physics processes more generally. Because the simulation results produced by GEANT3 and GEANT4 are nearly identical for many standard applications, both versions remain extensively employed and validated within the high-energy physics community. The middle layer constitutes the FairRoot core, which centrally manages the execution flow through the Run Manager. On one hand, the framework delivers managing classes that drive the execution of a simulation or reconstruction session, handle the Input/Output (I/O) to files, process parameter I/O, and build the geometry for a simulation from various input files. On the other hand, it provides essential base classes for detector handling, magnetic field definition, event generators for simulation sessions, and base task structures used for analysis sessions. Finally, the bottom layer contains the experiment-specific code. Historically, the code base was split into the base part called FairRoot and the experiment-specific parts, such as CbmRoot and PandaRoot. In this bottom tier, individual PANDA sub-detectors (e.g., MVD, STT, EMC) and their distinct digitization or track-finding algorithms are securely implemented by inheriting from the middle-layer core base classes. Using and extending the task mechanism of ROOT, it is possible to implement complex analysis tasks in a highly structured manner. Within this framework, FairTask serves as the fundamental class that facilitates the construction of a hierarchical tree of processing tasks. Derived from ROOT's base TTask class, it can elegantly contain multiple sub-tasks that are executed recursively. Consequently, highly sophisticated simulation and reconstruction programs can be dynamically assembled and executed simply by invoking the services of the top-level task or its specific sub-tasks.
The PandaRoot Software
47
Figure 2.17 depicts the data flow of the PandaRoot framework. The simulation process involves the generation of physics and background events using several event generators such as 'Particle Gun', EvtGen, DPM, PYTHIA, and UrQMD. The VMC is utilized for the transportation of the generated particles through the detectors, where they interact with the sensitive elements. The energy deposit resulting from these interactions is digitized to simulate future measurements of the experiments. Using the digitized output of the sinulation or experiment data, the hits can be reconstructed, followed by track finding, fitting, and particle identification to perform the physics analysis.

final_evidence.text: ¯ PANDA trigger and DAQ Because the high precision physics goals of the ¯ PANDA experiment require a substantial amount of data, the ¯ PANDA data acquisition (DAQ) system has to handle high data rates of up to 200 GB/ sec at an average interaction rate of 20 MHz [ 88 ]. To deal with the large fraction of background a sophisticated event filtering and trigger system are mandatory. One unique feature of ¯ PANDA is that no global hardware trigger will be used, but instead solely a partial reconstruction of the events will lead to the trigger decision. Every detector front end is running independently and employs feature extraction algorithms to select relevant data. It is collected by data concentrators and sent to a two stage event building network. Compute nodes reconstruct the reactions on the fly in order to form a trigger decision and write the interesting events to tape. To synchronize the DAQ system across all sub-detectors the synchronization of data acquisition (SODA) protocol[ 89 ] will be used. It offers a global clock with a jitter of less than 20 ps and timestamps coupled to the HESR beam structure. This way it is possible to assemble a complete event out of the information from individual detector components within the event building network.

• FairRoot handling the framework (data I/O, interfaces, infrastructure). The task
is to provide all steps of the data processing up to the physics analysis stage.
Data is stored in a ROOT ﬁle, using ROOT objects handling with chains, trees and
branches.
• DetectorRoot detector framework (detector simulations and data reconstruction).
For the Panda experiment such framework is called PandaRoot.
The PandaRoot framework user should add detector class implementations for the
transport model and reconstruction tasks, which are processing the data. A typical chain
of generating and processing of simulated data contains the following ingredients:
1. Event Generator:
The event generator produces in each event a set of particles according to the in-
vestigated physics reaction or detector studies. Particles are deﬁned by their type
and four-momentum, point of origin and time. Those properties are randomly
distributed by the selected model. In PandaRoot for this purpose several gener-
ators are available. The "BOX" generator provides a uniform distribution for all
variables. It also has possibility to choose a certain variable range. A generator
for single-channel generation is called EvtGen [63]. And the DPM [64] generator
provides the full description of all antiproton-proton reactions.
2. Transport Code (VMC):
The particle transport through matter is simulated by Geant [58],[59]. The Virtual
Monte-Carlo interface (VMC) allows to switch between the diﬀerent Geant ver-
sions as well as to introduce other packages. Each sub-detector has its own geom-
etry description (usually in ROOT format) and deﬁnition of the active and passive
elements. For all materials in which particles can interact according to physical
processes, such as ionization, showering or Cherenkov emission, they react with
the detector material and loss of energy is estimated. Interaction of particle with
the detector material (e.g position and energy loss) is saved in each event. This
data is called MCHits and it is accessible for the analysis of the performance of
the reconstruction steps.
3. Digitization:
All Monte-Carlo data is processed to model the detectors response. The threshold,
eﬃciency and ampliﬁcation can be adjusted according to the measurements of
real detector response. The digitized data formats in the simulation must be the
same as those obtained in a real implementation (a prototype detector or even
the ﬁnal setup). This data is called DigiHits and is used as input information for
reconstruction of the events.

Chapter4
Extraction of the luminosity
For the determination of the luminosity, the diﬀerential cross section in dependence of
the scattering angle has to be extracted from data. The data reconstruction includes
several necessary steps: ﬁnding and ﬁtting of the tracks of the elastically scattered
antiprotons and backtracking them to the interaction point in order to get rid of the
inﬂuence of the magnetic ﬁeld.
A complete simulation of the PANDA detector components and their response to
the passage of particles has been developed within the PandaRoot framework [57]. It
is designed that way that the same reconstruction and analysis algorithms will work on
the simulation output as well as on data. This chapter gives an overview of the frame-
work and describes all procedures related to the track reconstruction in the luminosity
detector and related performance studies.

PandaRoot framework layout
The software framework is a collection of software packages and tools for the descrip-
tion of the single detector components and the simulation of physics reactions. The
layout is organized such as to allow the re-use of well known programs and tools, com-
mon to particle and nuclear physics simulations. One basic concept of the framework
is its modularity, the possibility to switch algorithms and procedures at any point in
the chain of processes. Hence a set of interfaces and data input/output are provided to
connect all these tools properly.
Almost all experiments at the future FAIR facility are using the following features of
organization of their software packages:
• External Packages with the commonly used packages as Geant3 and Geant4 (prop-
agation of particles through matter written in Fortran [58] and C++ [59]), VMC

# Waveform-Generation

Base package allowing to simulate Waveforms of different pulseforms.

## Baseclasses
These interfaces/classes and simulators are used internally by the WaveformGeneration-Task/Process.

- [BSEmcAbsPulseshape](BSEmcAbsPulseshape.h): Pulseshape interface
- [BSEmcAbsWaveformModifier](BSEmcAbsWaveformModifier.h): Waveform modifier interface
- [BSEmcAbsWaveformSimulator](BSEmcAbsWaveformSimulator.h): Waveform simulator interface. The idea here is to sample from a **BSEmcAbsPulseshape** to create the main waveform and then to use several **BSEmcAbsWaveformModifier**s to add noise, digitize and clip the waveform.
- [BSEmcWaveformData](BSEmcWaveformData.h): Data storage for crystal (accumulates hits)
- [BSEmcWaveformBuffer](BSEmcWaveformBuffer.h): Buffer for waveform

### Waveform simulators
- [BSEmcFullStackedWaveformSimulator](BSEmcFullStackedWaveformSimulator.h): Fully functional Waveform simulator for single waveforms per crystal. Creates **BSEmcWaveform**.
- [BSEmcMultiWaveformSimulator](BSEmcMultiWaveformSimulator.h): Simulator for waveform with low and highgain signals. Creates **BSEmcMultiWaveform**.


## Waveform Generation
On a script or **MasterTask** level one would only interact with the
**BSEmcMCDepositToTimebasedWaveforms** (**FairTask** derived) or with **BSEmcWaveformGenerationProcess** (**PndProcess** derived).


- [BSEmcWaveformGenerationProcess](BSEmcWaveformGenerationProcess.h): A **PndProcess** to create **BSEmcMultiWaveform** out of **BSEmcMCDeposit** using a **BSEmcAbsWaveformSimulator**. Waveform form is defined by **BSEmcAbsPulseshape** and  additional waveform modifications (aka **BSEmcAbsWaveformModifier**) such as noise adding or digitizing are implemented again in  Detector subfolder).
**BSEmcAbsWaveformSimulator** is instantiated in an Emc Subdetector specific implementation of **BSEmcWaveformGenerationProcess**.

You can steer where to write the Waveforms and the WaveformData using **BSEmcWaveformGenerationProcess** via:
| attribute | description | setter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fWaveformBranchName | Output branch name for the **BSEmcMulitWaveform** data (default = BSEmcDataBranchNames::fgWaveformDataBranchName+fDetectorName)| *void SetWaveformBranchName(const TString &t_branchname)*  |
| fWaveformDataBranchName |  Output branch name for the **BSEmcWaveformData** data (default = BSEmcDataBranchNames::fgWaveformDataBranchName+fDetectorName)| *void SetWaveformDataBranchName(const TString &t_branchname)* |
| fActivateBuffering | Run the Waveform Generation Timebased, which means that **BSEmcMCDeposit**s are buffered for one crystal up to a certain time and then the waveform is generated with all **BSEmcMCDeposit**s (default = kFALSE) | *void RunTimebased(Bool_t t_timebased)* |
| fStoreWaves | Should the **BSEmcMulitWaveform** data be stored (default = kFALSE) | *void SetStorageOfData(Bool_t t_storeWaves)* |
| fStoreDataClass | Should the **BSEmcWaveformData** data be stored (default = kFALSE)  | *void StoreDataClass(Bool_t t_storeData)* |

**BSEmcAbsWaveformSimulator** is instantiated in an Emc Subdetector specific implementation of **BSEmcMCDepositToTimebasedWaveforms**.

You can steer where to write the Waveforms and the WaveformData using **BSEmcMCDepositToTimebasedWaveforms** or **BSEmcWaveformGenerationProcess** via:
| attribute | description | setter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fWaveformBranchName | Output branch name for the **BSEmcMulitWaveform** data (default = BSEmcDataBranchNames::fgWaveformDataBranchName+fDetectorName)| *void SetWaveformBranchName(const TString &t_branchname)*  |
| fWaveformDataBranchName |  Output branch name for the **BSEmcWaveformData** data (default = BSEmcDataBranchNames::fgWaveformDataBranchName+fDetectorName)| *void SetWaveformDataBranchName(const TString &t_branchname)* |
| fActivateBuffering | Run the Waveform Generation Timebased, which means that **BSEmcMCDeposit**s are buffered for one crystal up to a certain time and then the waveform is generated with all **BSEmcMCDeposit**s (default = kFALSE) | *void RunTimebased(Bool_t t_timebased)* |
| fStoreWaves | Should the **BSEmcMulitWaveform** data be stored (default = kFALSE) | *void SetStorageOfData(Bool_t t_storeWaves)* |

- [BSEmcExtractDigisFromWaveforms](BSEmcExtractDigisFromWaveforms.h): Task to extract Features from  **BSEmcMultiWaveform** to create **BSEmcDigi** using a **BSEmcAbsPSA** specifically implemented by each Emc Detector version of **BSEmcExtractDigisFromWaveforms**.

Usage inside the Code
Options in a ROOT macro
Running the software encloses a lot of algorithms and packages. A comprehensive overview is given in
Running Sequence
. For a quick way to set up everything it is recommended to familiarize with the
MasterTasks
. Developers also should have a look at the useful logging possibilities in
Using the Logger from Fair
.
Event Generation
¶
First stage is the event generation. It simulates the interaction of the antiproton beam with the target.
It does not include any interaction with the PANDA detector which is important for the decay of long living charged particles like hyperons.
Transport
¶
In the second stage the particles generated via the event generator are transported through the detector. This is done via either
Geant3
or
Geant4
which can be seamlessly selected via
VMC
.
In this stage the particle properties like their decay length, interaction with the detector material and fields are taken into account.
It creates a realistic picture about the processes taking place inside the detector. The output of this stage is
a Monte Carlo truth list of generated particles with their point of origin, momentum, charge and creation time, and, for each sub-detector, a list
of points where the particles have interacted with sensitive detector material, containing the time, position and lost energy at that point.
Digitization
¶
In the digitization stage the detector responds to the deposited charge in the sensitive volume is simulated.
In contains both the sensor properties as well as the readout electronics features of a subdetector.
The output should be a data stream matching with the one generated by the DAQ of the real PANDA experiment.
What is simulated and how detailed the simulation is, differs for each sub-detector.
Reconstruction
¶
The reconstruction is subdivided into two stages, the local reconstruction and the global reconstruction.
Local Reconstruction
¶
The local reconstruction is operating on the sub-detector data independently from each other and is part of the sub-detector code.
It translates the digitized detector data back into physical quantities like the translation from fired detector channel into a position in the detector,
or an ADC value back into an energy.
Global Reconstruction/Tracking
¶
Global reconstruction in PANDA mainly means reconstructing the track of charged particles from the measured hit points in the tracking detector.
This process happens again in two stages. The firs one is the track finding and pre-fitting stage. Here the hit points are sorted into
groups of hits which could belong to one track and a rough estimate of the track parameters like charge, momentum and position on track are calculated.
In the second stage a Kalman filter is used to improve the track parameters by taking also energy loss and multiple scattering into account
which is typically neglected in the pre-fitting stage.
Particle Identification
¶
The last stage before the analysis is the particle identification (PID). Here the tracks of the global reconstruction are combined with the measurements
of the PID detectors and the EMC and a probability for each stable particle species is calculated (e, pi, mu, K, p).
The complete information about one particle is then stored in a charged candidate. For those cluster in the EMC where no track is pointing to
an addition neutral candidate is created.
Analysis
¶
A analysis of a simulated physics channel or background data is performed using the Rho package.

61
(Virtual Monte-Carlo [60]), ROOT (Plotting, ﬁtting, graphics etc. [61]), Pythia [62]
and auxiliary tools
• FairRoot handling the framework (data I/O, interfaces, infrastructure). The task
is to provide all steps of the data processing up to the physics analysis stage.
Data is stored in a ROOT ﬁle, using ROOT objects handling with chains, trees and
branches.
• DetectorRoot detector framework (detector simulations and data reconstruction).
For the Panda experiment such framework is called PandaRoot.
The PandaRoot framework user should add detector class implementations for the
transport model and reconstruction tasks, which are processing the data. A typical chain
of generating and processing of simulated data contains the following ingredients:
1. Event Generator:
The event generator produces in each event a set of particles according to the in-
vestigated physics reaction or detector studies. Particles are deﬁned by their type
and four-momentum, point of origin and time. Those properties are randomly
distributed by the selected model. In PandaRoot for this purpose several gener-
ators are available. The "BOX" generator provides a uniform distribution for all
variables. It also has possibility to choose a certain variable range. A generator
for single-channel generation is called EvtGen [63]. And the DPM [64] generator
provides the full description of all antiproton-proton reactions.
2. Transport Code (VMC):
The particle transport through matter is simulated by Geant [58],[59]. The Virtual
Monte-Carlo interface (VMC) allows to switch between the diﬀerent Geant ver-
sions as well as to introduce other packages. Each sub-detector has its own geom-
etry description (usually in ROOT format) and deﬁnition of the active and passive
elements. For all materials in which particles can interact according to physical
processes, such as ionization, showering or Cherenkov emission, they react with
the detector material and loss of energy is estimated. Interaction of particle with
the detector material (e.g position and energy loss) is saved in each event. This
data is called MCHits and it is accessible for the analysis of the performance of
the reconstruction steps.
3. Digitization:
All Monte-Carlo data is processed to model the detectors response. The threshold,
eﬃciency and ampliﬁcation can be adjusted according to the measurements of
real detector response. The digitized data formats in the simulation must be the
same as those obtained in a real implementation (a prototype detector or even
the ﬁnal setup). This data is called DigiHits and is used as input information for
reconstruction of the events.

A comprehensive schematic structure of FairRoot is presented in Figure 2.16. As explicitly illustrated, the software architecture is intrinsically divided into three hierarchical layers: the underlying dependencies (top), the core framework (middle), and the experiment-specific implementations (bottom). The top layer comprises the foundational ROOT libraries and the Virtual Monte Carlo (VMC) [115] interface. Developed at CERN, ROOT provides a vast array of tools essential for high-energy physics, encompassing robust data analysis and performance simulation functionalities, thereby serving as the absolute bedrock of FairRoot. Working together with ROOT is the VMC, a widely utilized abstraction tool in high-energy physics. The VMC enables seamless access to various Monte Carlo transport engines without necessitating any alterations to the user's code, geometry, or detector descriptions. Presently, VMC supports the use of both GEANT3 [116] and GEANT4 [117], with support for FLUKA [118] currently under development. GEANT itself is the standard application suite for simulating the passage of particles through matter. It exists in two major iterations: GEANT3, which is a legacy system coded in FORTRAN, and GEANT4, a modern evolution written in C++ that employs an object-oriented design to implement physics processes more generally. Because the simulation results produced by GEANT3 and GEANT4 are nearly identical for many standard applications, both versions remain extensively employed and validated within the high-energy physics community. The middle layer constitutes the FairRoot core, which centrally manages the execution flow through the Run Manager. On one hand, the framework delivers managing classes that drive the execution of a simulation or reconstruction session, handle the Input/Output (I/O) to files, process parameter I/O, and build the geometry for a simulation from various input files. On the other hand, it provides essential base classes for detector handling, magnetic field definition, event generators for simulation sessions, and base task structures used for analysis sessions. Finally, the bottom layer contains the experiment-specific code. Historically, the code base was split into the base part called FairRoot and the experiment-specific parts, such as CbmRoot and PandaRoot. In this bottom tier, individual PANDA sub-detectors (e.g., MVD, STT, EMC) and their distinct digitization or track-finding algorithms are securely implemented by inheriting from the middle-layer core base classes. Using and extending the task mechanism of ROOT, it is possible to implement complex analysis tasks in a highly structured manner. Within this framework, FairTask serves as the fundamental class that facilitates the construction of a hierarchical tree of processing tasks. Derived from ROOT's base TTask class, it can elegantly contain multiple sub-tasks that are executed recursively. Consequently, highly sophisticated simulation and reconstruction programs can be dynamically assembled and executed simply by invoking the services of the top-level task or its specific sub-tasks.
The PandaRoot Software
47
Figure 2.17 depicts the data flow of the PandaRoot framework. The simulation process involves the generation of physics and background events using several event generators such as 'Particle Gun', EvtGen, DPM, PYTHIA, and UrQMD. The VMC is utilized for the transportation of the generated particles through the detectors, where they interact with the sensitive elements. The energy deposit resulting from these interactions is digitized to simulate future measurements of the experiments. Using the digitized output of the sinulation or experiment data, the hits can be reconstructed, followed by track finding, fitting, and particle identification to perform the physics analysis.

# Base

Common EMC functionality

## EmcPlotProcesses

A set of Processes dedicated to create plots for debugging. Instead of having to write Tasks over and over a BSEmcPlotProcess (specific for the Emc) was written, that fetches for a given Detector all possible branches. The writer of a PlotProcess only has to focus on what he wants and does not have to deal with the Branch-fetching

## EmcMC

All classes related to simulation (from ```BSEmcMCPoint``` to ```BSEmcDigi```(for the ideal digitizing)).


## EmcClustering

All Clustering related classes. Task, DataContainer, Parameter, Processes and Algorithms. Algorithms are more or less calculation modules e.g. how to calculate the Zernike moments, or the position of a cluster (linearly, logarithmically, etc.)


## EmcReco
Processes and Utility to form out of ```BSEmcCluster/SubCluster``` a ```BSEmcRecoHit```, a data class that contains all information of an Particle Hit in one of the EMC. This will close of the EmcReconstruction specifics and offers the PidCorrelator Stage an easy to use set of data.

## Timebased

All classes related to the timebased digitizing (aka ```BSEmcMCDeposit``` over ```BSEmcWaveform``` to ```BSEmcDigi```). It contains the base for the Waveform simulation to the Pulse Shape Analysis(PSA) (aka Feature Extraction). However, the subdetectors contain their own Waveform Simulation and PSA classes.

### Timesorting

Tools to reform event structure into timestream for Digis and Precluster

## EmcGeoParts

Utility classes to handle crystal position and neighbouring relations.

## EmcTools

Some useful general tools such as a Histogrammer or a Task to join branches into one.

# Missing things
- Digi Timeresolution is not set yet -> Bump/SubCluster time taken from central crystal. The DigiTimeCalibration is not documented well enough.

Chapter4
Extraction of the luminosity
For the determination of the luminosity, the diﬀerential cross section in dependence of
the scattering angle has to be extracted from data. The data reconstruction includes
several necessary steps: ﬁnding and ﬁtting of the tracks of the elastically scattered
antiprotons and backtracking them to the interaction point in order to get rid of the
inﬂuence of the magnetic ﬁeld.
A complete simulation of the PANDA detector components and their response to
the passage of particles has been developed within the PandaRoot framework [57]. It
is designed that way that the same reconstruction and analysis algorithms will work on
the simulation output as well as on data. This chapter gives an overview of the frame-
work and describes all procedures related to the track reconstruction in the luminosity
detector and related performance studies.
4.1
PandaRoot framework layout
The software framework is a collection of software packages and tools for the descrip-
tion of the single detector components and the simulation of physics reactions. The
layout is organized such as to allow the re-use of well known programs and tools, com-
mon to particle and nuclear physics simulations. One basic concept of the framework
is its modularity, the possibility to switch algorithms and procedures at any point in
the chain of processes. Hence a set of interfaces and data input/output are provided to
connect all these tools properly.
Almost all experiments at the future FAIR facility are using the following features of
organization of their software packages:
• External Packages with the commonly used packages as Geant3 and Geant4 (prop-
agation of particles through matter written in Fortran [58] and C++ [59]), VMC

================

A complete PandaRoot simulation consists of several separated simulation stages.

Event Generator
---------------

First stage is the event generator. It simulates the interaction of the antiproton beam with the target.
It does not include any interaction with the PANDA detector which is important for the decay of long living charged particles like hyperons.

In the second stage the particles generated via the event generator are transported through the detector. This is done via either `Geant3`_ or `Geant4`_

a Monte Carlo truth list of generated particles with their point of origin, momentum, charge and creation time, and, for each sub-detector, a list
of points where the particles have interacted with sensitive detector material, containing the time, position and lost energy at that point.

# Master Macros
These ROOT macros run a complete chain of a default PandRoot simulation. They employ the so-called Master run and Master Tasks, which are tools to provide default settings and operation modes.
It is not important where you store the macros. You may copy the whole folder to a place of your liking.
Keep in mid to source the
config.sh -p
script to set up each terminal you are using.
## First Steps
If you simply want to simulate & reconstruct some events with default settings you’ll need only 2 commands:
Starting with a simulation (here 100 events)
`
root
-l
-b
-q

Running Sequence
¶
A complete PandaRoot simulation consists of several separated simulation stages.
Event Generator
¶
First stage is the event generator. It simulates the interaction of the antiproton beam with the target.
It does not include any interaction with the PANDA detector which is important for the decay of long living charged particles like hyperons.
Several different event generators exist for the different interaction scenarios.
For a more detailed description see
Event Generators
.
Transport
¶
In the second stage the particles generated via the event generator are transported through the detector. This is done via either
Geant3
or
Geant4
which can be seamlessly selected via
VMC
.
In this stage the particle properties like their decay length, interaction with the detector material and fields taken into account. It creates a realistic picture about the processes taking place inside the detector. The output of this stage is
a Monte Carlo truth list of generated particles with their point of origin, momentum, charge and creation time, and, for each sub-detector, a list
of points where the particles have interacted with sensitive detector material, containing the time, position and lost energy at that point.

Here, 𝜖 𝑖 represents the geometrical acceptance map, 𝐵 𝑖 is the background term, and 𝑅 is the resolution function. The symbol ⊗ denotes the numerical convolution of the theoretical cross section with the detector resolution. By modeling these effects explicitly, the software ensures that the extracted parameters are free from detector-induced biases.
IP Alignment and Coordinate Transformation
A critical pre-processing step implemented in the framework is the alignment of the coordinate system. The standard laboratory frame assumes the interaction point is at (0 , 0 , 0). However, real beam operations imply a transverse offset ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 ).
The framework utilizes the full 3D tracking information available after the backpropagation step to determine this offset geometrically. For each back-propagated track, the Point of Closest Approach (POCA) relative to the nominal coordinate origin (0 , 0 , 0) (or given point ( 𝑥 𝑖 , 𝑦 𝑖 , 0) taken from other detectors) is calculated. This results in a distribution of interaction vertices in the transverse plane. The arithmetic mean of these POCA coordinates is identified as the measurement of the mean interaction point ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 , 0). Before the luminosity fit, a global coordinate transformation is applied to all track data:
This virtually shifts the detector system such that the interaction point coincides with the origin, restoring the azimuthal symmetry required for the 2D luminosity fit model.
Detector Response Modeling
The raw angular distribution measured by the LMD differs from the theoretical cross-section due to two distinct instrumental effects: the limited geometrical acceptance and the finite angular resolution. In the LuminosityFit framework, these effects are decoupled and treated sequentially using a forward-folding approach.
The Acceptance 𝜖 represents the probability that an elastic scattering event is successfully detected and reconstructed. Due to the planar geometry of the HV-MAPS, the acceptance structures (such as sensor edges, overlaps, and module gaps) are most naturally described in the projected angular coordinates ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ).
The acceptance map 𝜖 ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ) is generated via extensive Monte Carlo simulations. A sample of 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 single track events is generated utilizing a Box Generator and processed through the full Geant4 detector simulation and tracking chain to obtain the number of reconstructed tracks ( 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐 ) independence on the coordinates

For the LMD analysis, the Cellular Automaton algorithm is the preferred choice [92]. The implementation used in this work creates track candidates requiring hits in at least 3 out of 4 stations to ensure high efficiency while suppressing ghost tracks.
Track Fitting with GenFit
Once track candidates are found, their kinematic parameters must be estimated. The reconstruction utilizes the GenFit toolkit [130], which supports multiple fitting algorithms, most notably the General Broken Lines (GBL) [131, 132] fit and the Kalman Filter [133, 134].
General Broken Lines (GBL) The GBL algorithm constructs a trajectory from a sequence of thin scatterers. It is particularly powerful for detector alignment as it provides explicit access to the residuals of all measurements simultaneously.
Kalman Filter The Kalman filter is a recursive estimator that updates the track state vector ⃗ 𝑞 = ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧, 𝑝 𝑥 , 𝑝 𝑦 , 𝑝 𝑧 ) at each measurement plane. It is the preferred algorithm for track reconstruction due to its superior handling of complex material effects. Specifically, it incorporates deterministic energy dissipation governed by the Bethe-Bloch formula when particles traverse the detector sensors and support structures. Furthermore, the filter elegantly accounts for Multiple Coulomb Scattering (MCS) by treating it as stochastic process noise. This approach appropriately inflates the track's covariance matrix, accurately reflecting the accumulated spatial uncertainties induced by the detector's material budget.
For the determination of the luminosity, the Kalman Filter is selected as the primary fitting algorithm. This ensures that the final error estimates at the first detector layer are statistically rigorous, which is a prerequisite for the accurate back-propagation to the interaction point.
Back-Propagation to the Interaction Point
For luminosity determination, the physics observable is the scattering angle 𝜃 at the Interaction Point ( 𝑧 = 0), not at the detector ( 𝑧 ≈ 11 m). Between the IP and the LMD, the antiprotons traverse the stray field of the solenoid and the strong dipole magnet field, which deflects trajectories horizontally. To recover the true scattering angle, the fitted tracks must be propagated backwards using the GEANE track propagator [135, 136]. This step involves a subtle but critical assumption regarding the particle momentum.

The framework explicitly separates the geometrical masking (in 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ) from the physics smearing (in 𝜃 ), ensuring a rigorous description of the detector response.
3.6 Effects of Beam Properties
In the ideal mathematical description of elastic scattering, the interaction occurs at a singular point (0 , 0 , 0) and the antiproton beam vector is perfectly aligned with the 𝑧 -axis. However, the realistic PANDA beam conditions at the HESR introduce geometric and kinematic deviations. To achieve the target precision for the luminosity determination, these effects must be rigorously modeled to avoid systematic biases. They can be categorized into deterministic mean shifts, shift and tilt as illustrated in Figure 3.10, and stochastic broadening (Divergence). The IP Offset , shown in green, shifts the primary vertex position away from the nominal detector center, thereby breaking the azimuthal symmetry of the tracks. Furthermore, the Beam Tilt , shown in blue, causes a systematic angular deviation that strongly depends on the azimuthal angle 𝜑 .
IP Offset and Distribution
The interaction zone is defined by the spatial overlap of the antiproton beam and the target stream. This creates a distributed source rather than a point source. The framework treats the mean position (Offset) and the profile width of this distribution differently based on the detector's sensitivity. A transverse displacement ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 ) of the beam breaks the azimuthal symmetry of the detector acceptance. To determine this offset precisely, the Back-Propagation procedure is exploited as described in Section 3.4. After extrapolating the reconstructed tracks through the magnetic field back to the target region, the geometrical origin of each track is determined by calculating its Point of Closest Approach (POCA) to the nominal coordinate origin (0 , 0 , 0). The spatial distribution of these POCA points reflects the beam spot profile smeared by the resolution from reconstruction precision. Nevertheless, the Mean of this distribution provides the mean interaction vertex ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 , 0) with high precision ( 𝒪 (10 𝜇 m)). This measured position is then used to define the 'Beam Reference Frame'. All reconstructed quantities are calculated relative to this physically determined center, effectively removing the systematic bias induced by the beam offset.

The Luminosity Fit Framework

Designed with a strict Object-Oriented architecture, the framework prioritizes modularity and flexibility. It decouples the physics implementation from the numerical optimization engine and the data storage backend. This separation of concerns allows for the seamless interchange of interaction models (e.g., different cross section parametrizations) or minimization algorithms without modifying the core analysis logic.
Architectural Design
The framework is structured around a central orchestration layer, utilizing the Facade Design Pattern to manage the interaction between four abstract components:
Data Representation Layer: Experimental data and Monte Carlo simulations after the full track reconstruction procedure in Section 3.4 are encapsulated into a unified histogram interface. This abstraction layer handles the binning of the angular phase space in the projected angular coordinates ( 𝜃 𝑥 and 𝜃 𝑦 , defined as 𝜃 𝑥 ≈ 𝑝 𝑥 /𝑝 𝑧 and 𝜃 𝑦 ≈ 𝑝 𝑦 /𝑝 𝑧 for small angles) and provides coherent access to bin contents and statistical errors. By isolating the analysis from the underlying file format (e.g., ROOT Trees), the fit performance is optimized for high-statistics datasets.
Abstract Model Interface: The physics of the scattering process is defined through a generalized model interface. Concrete implementations (e.g., the DPM) provide the probability density functions (PDF). Crucially, this layer is responsible for the 'Forward-Folding' process: it accounts for the detector acceptance, which incorporates the beam shift effects, and convolves the theoretical cross section (as shown in Figure 3.4) with the detector resolution and beam smearing effects during the fit.
Estimator Strategy: The quantification of the agreement between the model and the data is handled by an interchangeable estimator component. While standard 𝜒 2 metrics are available for diagnostics, the primary analysis utilizes a Binned Log-Likelihood estimator. This approach is statistically required to correctly treat low-statistics bins in the high-| 𝑡 | tail of the distribution.
Minimization Backend: The numerical optimization of the likelihood function is delegated to an external engine wrapper. This design allows the framework to utilize robust third-party libraries (such as Minuit2 ) to find the global minimum in the multi-dimensional parameter space efficiently.

Figure 20 : Simulation model of the luminosity detector.
By looking at the complete flow-chart of the software package (figure 21 ) one can see the workflow of the LMD software. The LMD fit procedure, which determines the luminosity from the angular antiproton distribution, requires three essential inputs: the reconstructed tracks arising from the actual measured detector hits, the detector acceptance and the detector resolution. In order to obtain this information several data processing steps are required, that can be categorized into three stages.
alignment stage : At first in the so called alignment stage the misalignment of each individual sensor has to be detected with respect to its reference position in the ¯ PANDA coordinate system. The alignment itself consists of three parts, the alignment of the sensors on a module, the alignment of modules within a corridor and the alignment of the corridors to the global ¯ PANDA reference frame [ 102 ]. Usually the alignment procedure only has to be performed once after the detector has been physically undergone changes, i.e initial setup or retraction/insertion of the detector halves. While the first two alignment parts are crucial for the correct reconstruction of particle track parameters, the third part is elementary for correct determination of the displacement of the IP and the accelerator beam tilt.
acceptance and resolution parameterizations : As a second step the detector acceptance and detector resolution parameterization are computed by using a MC data sample and by using the IP position information from the first stage.
data reconstruction The third stage consists of the track reconstruction from the measured data, which has to be corrected for the misalignment of the sensors.
Note that the second and third step are only dependent on step 1 , hence they are not time-ordered with respect to each other. All three stages share the same track recon- struction software. Figure 22 provides a zoom-in into stage 3 of figure 21 . The complete reconstruction chain is separated into 6 steps, each performing a specific task going from the raw pixel data to the fully reconstructed track at the IP [ 98 ].
